'Ata' and many scholars said: its meaning is "fa-zanna an lan nudayyiqa 'alayhi" (he thought that We would not constrict him), from His words: ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:26), that is, He restricts it. And He said: ﴿And whose provision is restricted for him﴾ (al-Talaq 65:7).

Ibn Zayd said: it is an interrogative, meaning: "Did he think that We would not have power over him?"

'Awf related from al-Hasan that he said: its meaning is: "He thought that He would be unable to overpower his Lord, so He could not decree against him."

He said: It has reached me that when Yunus sinned, he set off angry at his Lord, and Satan led him astray until he thought that He would not have power over him.

He said: He had earlier merit and worship, but God refused to leave him to Satan, so He cast him into the belly of the fish. He remained in the belly of the fish for forty days and nights, and it was said: seven days, and it was said: three. God held back his soul and did not kill him there. He repented to his Lord in the belly of the fish and returned to himself, saying: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87), so God brought him out of the belly of the fish by His mercy.

'Awf said: It has reached me that he said: "And I built You a mosque in a place where no one had built one before me." The earlier interpretations are more fitting for the prophets and further from error.

﴿And he called out in the darknesses﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87): that is, the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. This is said by most exegetes. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd said: the darkness of the belly of the fish, then the darkness of the belly of the other fish that swallowed it in the darkness of the sea.

﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87). Muhammad ibn Qays said: Yunus said: "Indeed I have been of the wrongdoers" when I disobeyed You, and in everything I did, I did not worship anyone other than You.

Abu Hurayrah related from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "When God the Exalted willed to imprison Yunus in the belly of the fish, He revealed to the fish: 'Take him, but do not tear his flesh or break his bones.' It took him and then plunged down with him to its dwelling in the sea. When it reached the bottom of the sea, Yunus heard a sound and said to himself: 'What is this?' God revealed to him, while he was in the belly of the fish: 'This is the glorification of the creatures of the sea.' So he glorified God while in the belly of the fish, and the angels heard his glorification and said: 'O our Lord, we hear a faint sound in a strange land!' He said: 'That is My servant Yunus, who disobeyed Me, so I imprisoned him in the belly of the fish.' They said: 'The righteous servant from whom righteous deeds ascended to You every day and night?' He said: 'Yes.' Then they interceded for him, and He commanded the fish, and it cast him onto the shore, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And he was ailing﴾ (al-Saffat 37:145)." [Jami' al-Bayan al-Tabari: 17/107.]

Abu Hilal Muhammad ibn Sulayman related from Shahr ibn Hawshab from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Jibril came to Yunus (peace be upon them both) and said to him: "Go to [the note in the Isfahan copy adds: the people of Nineveh, and warn them that the punishment has drawn near to them]." He said: "Seek a way out." He said: "The matter is quicker than that." He became angry at that and went off to the ship, boarded it, and the ship was held back. They cast lots, and the lot fell upon him. The fish came, wagging its tail, and the fish was called: "We did not make Yunus your provision; We made you a refuge and a mosque for him." The fish swallowed him and carried him from that place until it passed with him by al-Ubulla, then passed with him over the Tigris, then went on until it cast him at Nineveh. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: Yunus's prophethood came only after the fish had spat him out. The evidence for this view is that God mentioned the story of Yunus in Surah al-Saffat, then followed it with His words: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ (al-Saffat 37:147).

Others said: rather, the story of the fish came after his calling his people and delivering to them the message of his Lord, as we have already explained.

Tafsir al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 83–94 (part 4 of 4):

﴿So We responded to him and delivered him from the distress. And thus do We deliver the believers﴾ from their distress when they call out to Us and supplicate Us.

Ali ibn Zayd narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: I heard Sa'd ibn Malik say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The Name of Allah by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked, He gives, is the supplication of Yunus ibn Matta." He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, is it specific to Yunus, or is it for the community of Muslims in general?" He said: "It is specific to Yunus, and general to the believers when they call upon it. Have you not heard the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then he called out in the darknesses﴾ up to His saying ﴿And thus do We deliver the believers﴾? And it is Allah's condition for whoever calls upon Him with it."

The recitation differed regarding His saying "nunji" (﴿nunji﴾). The majority read it with two nuns, the second of them sukun, from al-inja' (deliverance), meaning "We deliver." If it is asked: why was it written in the codices (al-masahif) with one nun? It is answered: because the second nun, when it became sukun and a sukun is not audible on the tongue, was dropped, just as they did with ﴿illa﴾, dropping the nun in ﴿lam-ja'alha﴾ or ﴿kashifa﴾ when it is assimilated into the lam. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, through the narration of Ibn Bakr, read ﴿nunji al-mu'minin﴾ with one nun, a shaddah on the jim, and sukun on the ya'. The grammarians differed regarding this reading. Some of them declared it correct and said: there is an implied element in it, meaning "nunji al-mu'minin," as one says "darab Zayd-an" meaning "darab al-darb Zayd-an" (he struck the striking, Zayd). The poet said:

"Even if a bitch gave birth to a puppy, the puppy would revile the dogs by that [act]."

He meant: it would revile them by that puppy, and it would revile the dogs.

They said: the ya' in "nunji" was made sukun just as they made the ya' sukun in "baqar," saying "baqarah" and similar words. The people of this reading only followed the codex because it is written with one nun.

Al-Qutaybi said: whoever reads with one nun and the shaddah intends "nunji" from al-tanjiyah (rescue), except that he assimilated and dropped one nun seeking lightness.

The grammarians said: this is weak, because the point of articulation of the nun is far from that of the jim. Among those who permitted this reading was Abu 'Ubayd. As for Abu Hatim al-Sijistani, he deemed it a solecism (lahn) and attributed its reader to ignorance, and said: "This is a solecism not permitted in the language, and one may not take such a verse as proof for the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, unless one says: 'wa-kadhalika najji al-mu'minin' (and thus He delivers the believers); and if it were recited thus, it would be correct. And Allah knows best."

﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, saying: "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors"﴾. Zakariyya supplicated his Lord, and said: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan), solitary (wahidan), without a child, without offspring, and grant me an heir." Then he referred the matter to Allah, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and You are the best of inheritors﴾. ﴿So We responded to him and granted him Yahya as a son, and We made his wife fit for him﴾, by making her fertile after she had been barren, as most exegetes said. Some of them said: she had a bad temperament, so He made her fit for him by granting her good character.

﴿Indeed they﴾, meaning the prophets whom He named in this surah,

﴿used to hasten to good deeds, and call upon Us with longing and fear﴾, in fear and hope: longing for the mercy of Allah and fear of the punishment of Allah. Al-A'mash read ﴿rughban wa-ruhban﴾ with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the ghayn and the ha', and both are dialects, like "al-suqm" and "al-suqm," "al-thukl" and "al-thukl," "al-nahl" and "al-nahl," "al-adam" and "al-adam."

﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾, subdued and humble.

﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾, who protected and preserved her private part from what Allah has forbidden. She is Maryam daughter of 'Imran. ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾: We commanded Jibril until he blew into the opening of her garment, and We caused that blowing to become the Messiah in her womb. The Spirit was attributed to Him in the sense of ownership and honour for Maryam and 'Isa, by singling her out with this attribution to Him.

﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾: a proof of the completeness of Our power and wisdom, a woman conceiving without touch of a male, and a child existing without a father. He said "ayatan" (a sign) and did not say "ayatayn" (two signs), because the meaning of the statement is "We made their condition and affair a sign for the worlds."

﴿Indeed this community of yours﴾, your religion, ﴿is one community﴾, one religion, which is Islam; thus He nullified all religions other than Islam. The root of "ummah" is a group that has one single aim, and by the Law it was made one community because its members gather upon one single aim through it. ﴿Ummah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial/absolute element (ʿalā al-qaṭʿ); Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿ummatun﴾ with a nominative, as a repetition (ʿalā al-takrīr).

﴿And I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾. ﴿But they divided their affair﴾ among themselves, meaning they differed in religion and became sects and factions. Then He said: ﴿each to Us they will return﴾, so We will recompense them for their deeds.

﴿So whoever does good deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort﴾: We will not nullify his deed nor deny it, but it will be appreciated and rewarded. ﴿And indeed We are recording it for him﴾: guardians of his deed.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 83–94 (part 1 of 4):

﴿And Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord…﴾ – the verse.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Ayyub was a man from the Romans. He was Ayyub ibn Amus ibn Razih ibn Rum ibn Ays ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and his mother was from the descendants of Lut ibn Haran. Allah the Exalted had chosen him, made him a prophet, and expanded the world for him. He owned the whole of al-Batheniyya in the land of al-Sham, its plains and its mountains with everything in them. He had every kind of wealth, including camels, cattle, horses and donkeys, in a number and abundance that no other man possessed. He had five hundred plough-lands, each worked by five hundred slaves, and each slave had a wife, children and property. Each plough-land yielded a she-ass for him, and each she-ass bore young, two, three, four, five or more. Allah the Exalted had given him a household and children, men and women. He was dutiful and pious, merciful to the poor, a guardian of widows and orphans, generous to guests, and a provider for the wayfarer. He was grateful for the blessings of Allah the Exalted and fulfilled the rights of Allah the Exalted. He was protected from the enemy of Allah, Iblis, so that Iblis could not inflict on him what he inflicts on the wealthy: pride, heedlessness, forgetfulness and being preoccupied with the world to the neglect of the command of Allah. With him were three men who had believed in him, confirmed him and recognised his merit: a man from Yemen called Alyafan, and two men from his land, one called Baldad and the other Safir. They were middle-aged men.

Wahb said: Jibril (peace be upon him) has a station before Allah the Exalted that none of the angels possesses in nearness and excellence. Jibril is the one who receives the speech. When Allah mentions a servant with good, Jibril receives it, then Mika'il receives it from him, and the angels brought near surround the Throne. When this spreads among the angels brought near, the prayer for that servant becomes the prayer of the inhabitants of the heavens. When the angels of the heavens pray for him, they descend with the prayer to the angels of the earth. [[In the Isfahan copy: "From the inhabitants of the heavens the prayer descended upon him to the angels of the earths."]] Iblis, may Allah curse him, was not barred from any of the heavens. He could stand in them wherever he wished, and from there he reached Adam when Allah expelled him from the Garden. He continued to ascend through the heavens until Allah raised Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him), and then he was barred from four of them, though he could still ascend through three. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), he was barred from the remaining three, so he and his armies are barred from all the heavens until the Day of Resurrection, ﴿except one who steals a hearing, and is pursued by a clear flame﴾ [[Al-Hijr: 18.]].

He said: Iblis heard the angels responding with prayer upon Ayyub, at the time when Allah mentioned him and praised him. Envy and resentment overtook him, and he ascended swiftly until he stood at the place in the heaven where he used to stand. He said: "O my God, I considered Your servant Ayyub, and I found that You have blessed him and he has thanked You, You have granted him well-being and he has praised You. Then You have not tested him with hardship or affliction. I stand surety for You: if You strike him with affliction, he will surely disbelieve in You and forget You." Allah the Exalted said to him: "Go, for I have given you power over his wealth." The enemy of Allah then swooped down until he reached the earth. He gathered the demons, the strong ones and their chieftains, and said to them: "What strength and knowledge do you have? For I have been given power over the wealth of Ayyub, which is a grievous calamity and a trial that men cannot bear."

A demon from among them said: "I have been given such strength that if I wish, I can turn into a whirlwind of fire, and burn everything I touch." Iblis said to him: "Go to his camels and their herders." He went to the camels at the time when they had lowered their heads and were settled in their pastures. People did not notice until a fiery whirlwind rose from under the earth, blowing scorching winds from it. No one approached it without being burned. It continued to burn the camels and their herders until it had consumed all of them. When it finished, Iblis appeared in the form of one of the herdsmen and went to Ayyub, and found him standing and praying. He said: "O Ayyub." He said: "Here I am." He said: "Do you know what your Lord, whom you chose and worship, has done with your camels and their herders?" Ayyub said: "It is His property. He lent it to me, and He has more right to it; when He wishes, He takes it back. Long ago I prepared my wealth and my soul for its perishing."

Iblis said: "Your Lord sent down fire from the heaven upon them, and they and all their herders were burned. The people were left stunned, standing over them in wonder. Some said: 'Ayyub did not worship anything, and he was only in delusion.' Others said: 'If the god of Ayyub could do anything, he would have protected his friend.' And others said: 'Rather, it is He who did what He did, to gladden his enemy and grieve his friend.'"

Ayyub said: "Praise be to Allah, who gave me and who took from me. I came out naked from my mother's womb, I will return naked to the earth, and I will be gathered naked to Allah the Exalted. It is not fitting for you to rejoice when He lent you something, and to lament when He takes back His loan. Allah has more right to you and to what He gave you. If Allah had known good in you, O servant, He would have received your soul along with those souls, reward for me in you, and I would have become a martyr. But He knew evil in you, so He delayed you [[In the Isfahan copy: "so He expelled you."]] and freed you from affliction, as chaff is separated from pure wheat."

Iblis, may Allah curse him, returned to his companions, humiliated and abased, and said: "What strength do you have? For I did not reach his heart." A demon from among their chieftains said: "I have such strength that if I wish, I can cry out with a voice that no living creature hears without its soul departing [[In the Isfahan copy: "its life-breath."]]." Iblis said to him: "Go to the sheep and their herders." He went to the sheep and their herders, and when he reached the middle of them, he shouted a cry that made them all collapse dead together, and their shepherds died too. Then Iblis went out in the form of the steward of the herdsmen, and came to Ayyub while he was standing and praying. He said to him the first words, and Ayyub gave him the first answer.

Then Iblis returned to his companions and said to them: "What strength do you have? For I did not reach Ayyub's heart." A demon from among their chieftains said: "I have such strength that if I wish, I can turn into a violent wind that scatters everything I pass over, until I leave nothing." Iblis said to him: "Go to the ploughlands and the tillage." He went to them at the time when the oxen had been yoked and were ploughing in the fields, with their young grazing. They did not notice until a violent wind blew and scattered everything of that, until it was as if it had never existed. Then Iblis went out in the form of the steward of the tillage, and came to Ayyub while he was standing and praying. He said to him the same as his first words, and Ayyub gave him the same answer as his first answer. Iblis kept striking his wealth, one portion after another, until he went through all of it. Whenever the destruction of one of his possessions reached him, he praised Allah, extolled Him well, was content with the decree, and prepared himself to be patient in affliction, until no wealth remained to him.

When Iblis saw that he had destroyed his wealth and had gained nothing from him, he ascended swiftly until he stood at the place where he used to stand, and said: "My God, Ayyub thinks that You did not provide for him through himself and his children, so You will give him wealth. Will You give me power over his children? For that is a misleading trial and a calamity before which the hearts of men cannot stand, and their patience cannot endure it."

Allah the Exalted said: "Go, for I have given you power over his children." The enemy of Allah swooped down until he came to the sons of Ayyub, who were in their palace. He continued shaking them until it collapsed from its foundations. Then he began to strike its walls, some against others, and pelted them with wood and stones, until he had mutilated them in every way. He raised the palace with them inside, turned it over, and they were left upside down. Then he went to Ayyub in the form of the teacher who used to instruct them in wisdom, wounded, with a split face, blood and brains flowing. He informed him of this and said: "O Ayyub, if only you had seen your sons, how they were tortured and turned over, so that they were upside down on their heads, their blood and brains flowing from their noses, their eyelids and their bodies. If only you had seen how their bellies were split and their intestines scattered, it would have broken your heart." He kept saying this and similar things and softening him, until Ayyub softened, wept, took a handful of dust and put it on his head. Iblis rejoiced at this, and ascended swiftly, delighted with what had happened from Ayyub's lament. Then Ayyub did not delay before he returned to himself and saw clearly, so he sought forgiveness, and the angels who were his companions ascended with his repentance. They raced Iblis to Allah, and He knows best. Iblis stood there, shamed and humiliated, and said: "O my God, Ayyub's loss of wealth and children was only made light for him because he thinks You did not provide for him through himself. You will restore to him wealth and children. Will You give me power over his body? How can You promise that, if You test him in his body, he will surely forget You, disbelieve in You, and deny Your blessing."

Allah the Exalted said: "Go, for I have given you power over his body. But you have no authority over his tongue, his heart or his mind." Allah the Exalted knew best about him. He only gave him power over him out of mercy, to magnify his reward, to make him a lesson for the patient and a reminder for the worshippers, so that whenever affliction befalls them they might take Ayyub as an example in patience and in hope of reward.

The enemy of Allah, Iblis, swooped down swiftly and found Ayyub prostrating. He hastened before he raised his head [[In the Isfahan copy there is an addition: "from the prostration."]] and came at him from the ground, at the place of his face. He blew into his nostril a blast from which his body caught fire. He was stricken, and from his horn to his foot there broke out pustules like the tails of sheep, and an itching came upon him that he could not control. He scratched with his nails until they all fell off. Then he scratched with rough hair-cloths until he cut himself. Then he scratched with pottery and rough stones, and he kept scratching until his flesh decayed, was cut, changed and stank.

The people of the town drove him out and placed him on a rubbish heap, and made a shelter for him. All of Allah's creatures abandoned him except his wife, who was Rahma bint Ifra'im ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub. She used to go to him to bring what would benefit him and what he needed. When the three companions of his, namely Alyafr, Yaldad and Safar, saw what Allah had afflicted him with, and that they had abandoned him without abandoning his religion, they went to him after his affliction had lasted long. They reproached him and blamed him, and said: "Repent to Allah the Exalted from the sin for which you have been punished." He said: "A young man who had believed in him and confirmed him was present with them, and he said to them: 'You have spoken, O elders, and you were more entitled to speak because of your age. But you have left out a better saying than the one you said, a more correct opinion than the one you held, and a finer course than the one you adopted. The rights and the protection that you owed were better than what you have described. Do you know, O elders, the right of the one whom you have belittled, and the sanctity of the one whom you have violated, and who is the man you have blamed and accused? Do you not know that Ayyub is the prophet of Allah, His chosen one, and the purest of the people of the earth today? Then you do not know, or Allah has not informed you, that He has been displeased with any aspect of him since what befell him until this day of yours, nor that He has taken from him any of the honour with which He honoured him, nor that Ayyub has departed from the truth during the whole time you have been with him until this day of yours. Even if affliction is what has lowered him in your eyes and placed him in your souls, you know that Allah the Exalted tests ﴿the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [4:69]. Then His testing of them is not proof of His displeasure with them, nor is it a sign of their wretchedness; rather it is honour and a choice for them. If Ayyub were not in this station with Allah, other than being a brother whom you chose for companionship, it would not be fitting for a forbearing person to rebuke his brother in affliction, to reproach him for misfortune, or to blame him for what he does not know. He is in distress and grief, but he should show mercy to him, weep with him, ask forgiveness for him, grieve with his grief, and guide him to the right course of his affairs. Whoever is ignorant of this is neither wise nor rightly guided. So fear Allah, O elders, for the greatness, majesty and remembrance of death in Allah's presence should cut off your tongues and break your hearts.

Do you not know that there are servants of Allah whom fear has silenced, not from incapacity or dumbness, and that they are eloquent, articulate, noble, friends of Allah, who know Allah and His days? But when they remember the greatness of Allah, their tongues are cut off, their skins shiver, their hearts break, and their minds are overcome, out of magnifying, honouring and glorifying Allah. When they recover from that, they hasten to Allah with pure deeds, considering themselves to be among the wrongdoers and sinners, though they are pure and innocent. They consider themselves among the negligent and remiss, though they are clever and strong. But they do not regard their great deeds as great for Allah, nor are they content with little for Allah, nor do they boast of their deeds to Him. They are terrified, dismayed, humble and submissive.'"

Ayyub said: "Allah the Exalted plants wisdom through mercy in the heart of the young and the old. When it takes root in the heart, Allah makes it appear on the tongue. Wisdom does not come from age or grey hair, nor from long experience. If Allah makes a servant wise in youth, he does not lose his standing among the wise, who see upon him the light of honour from Allah the Exalted."

Then Ayyub turned to the three and said: "You came to me in anger. You were frightened before you were made afraid, and you wept before you were struck. How would it be with me if I told you to give charity from your wealth on my behalf? Perhaps Allah would free me, or offer a sacrifice on my behalf, perhaps Allah would accept it and be pleased with me. You have been impressed with yourselves, and you thought you were punished for your good deeds. Then you were arrogant and grew proud. If you had looked at what is between you and your Lord, and then been honest, you would have found faults of yours that Allah has covered with the well-being with which He clothed you. I was once respected by men, my words were heard, my right was recognised, and I dealt justly with my opponent. Today I have no opinion and no speech with you, for you were harder on me than my calamity."

Then he turned away from them, and turned to his Lord, seeking help from Him and humbling himself before Him, and said: "My Lord, why did You create me? Would that when You hated me, You had not created me. Would that I had been a menstrual discharge that my mother cast out. Or would that I had known the sin I committed and the deed I did, so that You would have turned Your noble face away from me. If You had let me die and joined me to my fathers, death would have been more beautiful for me. Was I not a home for the stranger, a refuge for the poor, a guardian for the orphan, and a protector for the widow?

My God, I am a humble servant. If I do well, the favour is Yours, and if I do wrong, my punishment is in Your hand. You have made me a target for affliction and a mark for trials. An affliction has fallen upon me which, if You had sent it upon a mountain, it would have been too weak to bear. How then can my weakness bear it? My God, my fingers have been cut off; I lift a morsel of food with both my hands, and they barely reach my mouth, and only with great effort. My uvula and the flesh of my head have fallen away, so that there is no barrier between my ears, and one can see the other. My brain flows from my mouth. The hair of my eyes has fallen out as though my face had been burned with fire, and my eyeballs hang down upon my cheeks. My tongue has swelled until it filled my mouth, so that whatever food I put into it chokes me. My lips swelled until the upper one covered my nose and the lower one covered my chin. My intestines in my belly have been cut; when food enters me, it comes out as it went in, and I feel nothing and gain nothing from it. The strength of my legs has gone, so that they are like two water-skins which I can barely carry. My wealth has gone, and I ask with my palm, and those whom I used to support feed me a single morsel, which they then grant me as a favour and reproach me for. My children have died, and if any of them had remained, he would have helped me in my affliction and benefited me. My family has grown weary of me, my relatives have disowned me, my acquaintances have turned strange to me, my friend has turned away from me, my companions have severed ties with me, my rights have been denied, and my kindnesses forgotten. I cry out and they do not cry back, I apologise and they do not excuse me. I called my servant and he did not answer me, I pleaded with my maidservant and she did not have mercy on me. [[In the Isfahan copy there is an addition: "Your bounty is what humiliated me and made me despised, and Your authority is what made me sick."]] My body has become emaciated. If my Lord were to remove the awe in my chest and loosen my tongue, so that I could speak with all my mouth, then indeed it would be fitting for a servant to plead his case on his own behalf. I would hope then that He would heal me from what I have, [[In the Isfahan copy: "punish me"]] but He has cast me away and kept Himself distant from me. He sees me and I do not see Him; He hears me and I do not hear Him. He does not look at me so as to have mercy on me, nor draw near to me so as to bring me close. So I speak of my innocence and argue on my own behalf."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 83–94 (part 2 of 4):

When Ayyub and his companions said that, a cloud overshadowed him, so that his companions thought it was a punishment. Then he was called from it: "O Ayyub, indeed Allah says: Behold, I have come near to you and have never ceased to be near you. So stand up and state your excuse, speak in your own defense, argue on your own behalf, gird up your loincloth and stand in the station of a mighty one, for it is not fitting for me to be disputed with except by a mighty one like me, and it is not fitting that anyone dispute with me except one who can place the flute in the mouth of the lion, the kids in the mouth of the phoenix, and the bridle in the mouth of the dragon, who can measure a measure of light, weigh a weight of wind, tie a bundle of the sun, and return yesterday. Your soul has deluded you into a matter that does not reach the level of your strength. Had you, when it deluded you and invited you to it, remembered what aim you were aiming at with yourself!

Did you wish to dispute with me with your mouth, or to argue with me with your speech, or did you wish to defy me with your weakness? Where were you with me on the day I created the earth and set it upon its foundation? Did you know by what measure I determined it, or were you with me stretching out its edges? Do you know what lies beyond its corners, or upon what its sides were placed? Was it by your obedience that the earth carries water, or by your wisdom was the earth a covering for the water? Where were you with me on the day I raised the heaven as a roof in the air, not with unattached ropes, nor held by support from beneath? Could your wisdom reach the point of making its light flow, or of setting its stars in motion, or of making its night and day differ by your command?

Where were you with me on the day I subjected the seas and caused the rivers to gush forth? Did your power hold back the waves of the seas within their bounds, or did your power open the wombs when their term was reached? Where were you with me on the day I poured water upon the dust and set up the towering mountains? Do you have an arm that can bear their weight? Or do you know how much of a weight is in them? Or where is the water that I sent down from the sky? Do you know whether it is a mother who bears it or a father who fathers it? Was it your wisdom that counted the drops and divided the provisions, or your power that stirs the clouds and covers them with water? Do you know what the sounds of thunder are, or from what thing the lightning flashes? Have you seen the depth of the sea, or do you know what lies beyond the air, or have you stored up the spirits of the dead? Do you know where the treasury of snow is, or where the storehouses of hail are, or where the mountains of hail are? Do you know where the treasury of night is in the day, and where the treasury of day is in the night, and where the path of light is, and in what language the trees speak, and where the treasury of the wind is? And how do locks restrain it?

And who placed intellects in men? Who split hearing? Who made the angels humble before His kingship, subdued the tyrants by His might, and apportioned the provision of beasts by His wisdom? Who apportioned to the lion its sustenance, taught the bird its livelihood, and made it tender toward its young? Who freed the wild beast from servitude and made the wilderness its dwelling, so that it is not made familiar by sounds and does not fear the powerful? Or did your wisdom make its mothers tender toward it, until they bring forth food for it from their bellies and prefer it with life over their own souls? Or by your wisdom does the eagle see with far-reaching sight and go to the places of the slain?

Where were you with me on the day I created Yahmut, who lies in the cleft of the dust, and the al-Wathbān (in the Isfahan copy: al-Wahl), who carry the mountains, the villages and the settlements? Their ears are like tall pine trees, their heads are like heaps of mountains, and the veins of their thighs are like pillars of copper. Did you fill their skins with flesh, or did you fill their heads with brains? Did you have any share in their creation, or do you have a strength by which two hands could overcome them? Does your power reach the point of placing your hand upon their heads, or of sitting for them on a path to hold them back or to turn them away from their strength? Where were you on the day I created for the dragon its provision in the sea and its dwelling in the clouds? Its eyes blaze with fire, its nostrils belch smoke, its ears are like the rainbow, from them flames erupt like a whirlwind of dust, its belly burns, its soul is ablaze, and its foam is glowing coals like rocks. The grinding of its teeth is like the sounds of thunderbolts, the gaze of its eyes is like the flash of lightning. Armies pass by it while it reclines, and nothing frightens it. There is no joint in it like iron; to it, iron is like clay, and copper is like threads. It does not fear arrows, nor does it feel the impact of rocks on its body. It moves through the air like a sparrow and destroys everything that passes by it. Will you seize it with your snare, or place a bridle in its jaws? Can you count its lifespan, or do you know its sustenance, or do you know what it has ruined from the earth, and what it will ruin of its remaining life?

Can you withstand its anger when it is angry, or can you command it so that it obeys you? Blessed is Allah, the Exalted."

Ayyub said: "I have fallen short of this matter which has been presented to me. Would that the earth had split open and I had gone into it, and that I had not spoken anything that angers my Lord. Affliction has gathered upon me, my God. You have made me like an enemy, though you used to honor me and knew my sincere counsel. You know that all that you have mentioned is the work of your hands and the design of your wisdom, and greater than this. Whatever you will, you do. Nothing overpowers you, no hidden thing is concealed from you, and no absent thing is absent from you. Who is this who imagines he can keep a secret from you, while you know what passes through the hearts? I have known from you in this trial of mine what I did not know, and when I tested your command I feared more than I used to fear. I used to hear of your might by hearsay, but now it is by the sight of the eye. I spoke when I spoke only so that you would excuse me, and I was silent when I was silent only so that you would have mercy on me. It was a word that slipped; I will not return to it. I have placed my hand over my mouth, bitten my tongue, pressed my cheek to the dust, and put my face into it, for my little ones, and I have been silent as my sin silenced me. So forgive me what I said, for I will not return to anything that you dislike from me."

Allah, glorified is He, said: "O Ayyub, my knowledge has been carried out concerning you, and my mercy has preceded my anger. Since you have erred, I have forgiven you. I have restored to you your family and your wealth, and their like with them, so that it may be a sign for those after you, an admonition for the people of trials, and a reward for the patient. Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink, in it is your healing. Offer a sacrifice for your companions and ask forgiveness for them, for they have disobeyed me concerning you."

He struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth for him, and he entered it and bathed, and Allah removed from him all the affliction that was on him. Then he came out and sat down. His wife came and began to look for him in his resting place, but she did not find him, so she stood up like one bereaved, bewildered and perplexed, and said: "O servant of Allah, do you have any knowledge of the afflicted man who was here?" He said to her: "Would you recognize him if you saw him?" She said: "Yes, why would I not recognize him?" So he smiled and said: "I am he." She recognized him by his smile, and embraced him.

Ibn Abbas said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Abdullah, I did not part from his embrace until every property and child they had passed by them." That is His saying: "And Ayyub, when he called upon his Lord: Indeed, harm has touched me." [Lengthy version in Tafsir al-Tabari: 17/76 to 90.]

The scholars differed concerning the time of his call, the cause for which he said "Indeed, harm has touched me," and the duration of his affliction.

Al-Imam Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Sahl al-Masarkhusi related to us by dictation on Friday in the year 384 [AH], saying: Abu Talib Umar ibn al-Rabi ibn Sulayman al-Khashshab informed us in Egypt, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub al-Allaf related to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Maryam related to us, saying: Nafi' ibn Yazid related to us, from Uqayl, from Shihab, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ayyub, the Prophet of Allah, remained in his affliction for eighteen years. Both the near and the distant abandoned him, except two men from among his brothers who used to come to him in the morning and in the evening. One of them said to his companion one day: 'By Allah, Ayyub has committed a sin that no one among the worlds has committed.' His companion said to him: 'And what is that?' He said: 'For eighteen years Allah has not had mercy on him so as to remove what is upon him.'

When they came to Ayyub, the man could not restrain himself until he mentioned that. Ayyub said: 'I do not know what the two of them are saying, except that Allah, glorified is He, knows that I used to pass by two men quarreling, and they would mention Allah, glorified and exalted is He. So I would return to my house and make expiation for them, out of dislike that they should mention Allah except in what is right.'"

[Narrated in Musnad Abi Ya'la: 6/299.]

He said: "He used to go out for his need, and when he had finished his need, his wife would take his hand until he reached home. One day he was late for her, and it was revealed to Ayyub in his place: 'Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink' [Surah Sad: 42]. She waited for him and went out looking, and he came toward her, Allah having removed from him all the affliction, and he was better than he had ever been. When she saw him she said: 'Have you seen the Prophet of Allah, the afflicted one?' He said: 'I am he.' He had two threshing floors: a threshing floor for wheat and a threshing floor for barley. Allah, glorified is He, sent two clouds. When one of them was over the wheat threshing floor, it poured gold into it until it overflowed, and the other poured silver into the barley threshing floor until it overflowed."

Al-Hasan said: "Ayyub lay cast upon a dunghill, a refuse heap of the Children of Israel, for seven years and some months, with beasts moving about on him."

Wahb said: "Ayyub did not have a skin disease. What came out of him was like the breasts of women, and then it would burst."

Al-Hasan said: "He had no wealth left, no child, no friend, and no one to draw near to him except a compassionate woman who stayed with him. She gave alms and came to him, and when he praised Allah, she praised Allah as well. Ayyub, for his part, never ceased from the remembrance of Allah, glorified is He, and from praising Him, and from patience under what He had tried him with. Then the enemy of Allah, Iblis, cried out a cry by which he gathered his armies from all regions of the earth, in distress at Ayyub's patience. When they gathered to him they said: 'What is your distress?' He said: 'This servant has defeated me. I asked my Lord to give me power over his wealth and children, so I left him no wealth, and he did not increase in that except in patience and praise of Allah, glorified is He. Then I was given power over his body, and I left him a sore cast on the dunghill of the Children of Israel, approached by none except his wife. I have been disgraced by my Lord, so I seek your help that you may assist me against him.' They said to him: 'Where is your cunning? Where is your work by which you destroyed those who came before?' He said: 'All of that has come to nothing with Ayyub. So advise me.' They said: 'We advise you. Do you recall Adam when you expelled him from Paradise?' He said: 'Through his wife.' They said: 'Then deal with Ayyub through his wife, for he cannot bring himself to disobey her, and no one draws near to him except her.' He said: 'You are right.' So he set off until he came to his wife while she was selling charity. He appeared to her in the form of a man and said: 'Where is your husband, O servant of Allah?' She said: 'There he is, scratching his sores, with beasts moving about on his body.' When he heard her, he hoped that she would utter a word of distress. So he whispered to her and reminded her of the blessings and wealth she had been in, and reminded her of Ayyub's beauty and youth, and of the harm he was now in, and that this would never end for them."

Al-Hasan said: "So she cried out. When she cried out, he knew that she had become distressed. He brought her a kid and said: 'Let this be slaughtered for me, and Ayyub will be healed.'"

He said: "She came crying out: 'O Ayyub, how long will your Lord torment you? Will He not have mercy on you? Where is the wealth? Where are the livestock? Where are the children? Where is the friend? Your fine complexion has changed and become like ash. Where is your beautiful body, which has decayed and in which beasts move about? Slaughter this kid and be at ease.'"

Ayyub said: "The enemy of Allah has come to you, blown into you, and you answered him?! Woe to you! Do you see what you weep over, what you mention of what we had of wealth, children and health? Who gave them to us?" She said: "Allah." He said: "How long did He let us enjoy them?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "And since when has Allah tested us with this affliction?" She said: "Since seven years and some months." He said: "Woe to you! By Allah, you have not been just nor fair to your Lord! Why did you not endure? This affliction with which our Lord has tried us would have lasted eighty years, just as we were in ease for eighty years. By Allah, if Allah heals me, I will certainly lash you a hundred lashes. You commanded me to slaughter for other than Allah? Your food and drink that you have brought me are forbidden to me, after you have said this to me. Begone from me, and let me not see you!" So he drove her away, and she left. When Ayyub looked and saw that his wife had been driven away, and that he had no food, no drink, and no friend, he fell down prostrate and said: "My Lord, harm has touched me," and then he returned that matter to his Lord and said: "And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." It was said to him: "Raise your head, for We have answered you. Strike with your foot." So he struck with his foot, and a spring gushed forth, and he bathed in it, and there remained on him no visible sore from a beast except that it fell off. Allah removed every pain and every sickness, his youth and beauty returned to him, better than they had ever been and more excellent than they had ever been. Then he struck his foot again, and another spring gushed forth, and he drank from it, and no disease remained in his belly except that it came out. He stood up healthy and was clothed in a fine garment.

He said: "He began to look around and saw nothing of his family or wealth that was not doubled for him by Allah. By Allah, it has been related to us that the water he bathed in splashed onto his chest as golden locusts. He began to gather them in his hand, and it was revealed to him: 'O Ayyub, have I not made you rich?' He said: 'Yes, but it is Your blessing; who could be satisfied with it?' He went out and sat down on an elevated place. Then his wife said: 'Do you see, if he had driven me away, to whom would he have entrusted his food? Let him die of hunger and be eaten by beasts! I will certainly go back to him.' So she returned to him, but she could see no dunghill, nor the condition that had been. Matters had changed, so she began to walk about where the dunghill had been, weeping, while Ayyub watched her."

He said: "She was afraid of the man in the garment, and did not dare to go to him to ask him about him. So Ayyub sent for her and called her, and said: 'What do you want, O servant of Allah?' She wept and said: 'I want that afflicted man who was cast on the dunghill. I do not know whether he was lost or what became of him.'

Ayyub said to her: 'What was it you did?' She wept and said: 'I want my husband. Have you seen him?' He said: 'Would you recognize him if you saw him?' She said: 'Could anyone who saw him be unaware of him?' Then she began to look at him, fearing him. Then she said: 'Indeed, he was the one most like you among the creatures of Allah, when he was healthy.' He said: 'I am Ayyub, whom you commanded to slaughter for Iblis. I obeyed Allah and disobeyed the devil, and I called upon Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and He returned to me what you see.'"

Ka'b said: "Ayyub remained in his affliction for seven years."

Wahb said: "Ayyub remained in that affliction for three years, not one day more. When Ayyub had overcome Iblis and he could do nothing to him, he appeared to Ayyub's wife in a form not like the form of the children of Adam in bone, body, or beauty, upon a mount that was not one of the mounts of men, possessing majesty, splendor and beauty. He said to her: 'Are you the wife of this afflicted man?' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you recognize me?' She said: 'No.' He said: 'I am the god of the earth, and I am the one who did to your companion what he did, because he worshipped the god of the heaven and left me, and so he angered me. If he had prostrated to me one single prostration, I would have restored to him and to you all that you had of wealth and children, for it is with me.' Then he showed them to her in the form in which she saw them, in the valley where she had met him."

Wahb said: "I have also heard that he only said: 'If your companion had eaten food without saying the name of Allah over it, he would have been healed of what he has of affliction.' And Allah knows best. Iblis, may Allah curse him, wanted to come to him through her."

It has been reported in some books that Iblis said to Rahmah: "If you wish, prostrate to me one single prostration, and I will restore to you your wealth and children, and cure your husband." She returned to Ayyub and informed him of what he had said to her and what she had seen. He said: "The enemy of Allah has come to you to tempt you away from your religion." Then he swore that if Allah healed him, he would certainly strike her a hundred lashes.

At that point he said: "Harm has touched me, from Iblis's hope for a prostration to me, which would violate my sanctity, and from his calling her and me to disbelief." They said: "Then Allah, glorified is He, had mercy on the wife of Ayyub for her patience with him in the affliction, and lightened it for her. He intended to free Ayyub from his oath, so He commanded him to take a bundle of branches and strike with it one blow, as Allah, glorified is He, said: 'And take in your hand a bundle and strike with it, and do not break your oath' [Surah Sad: 44], and so on."

Wahb and others said: "Ayyub's wife used to earn for him and work for people and bring him his food. When the affliction lengthened for them both, and people grew weary of her and no longer employed her, she sought something for him to eat one day, but she found nothing. So she cut off a lock of her hair and sold it for a loaf of bread, and brought it to him. He said to her: 'Where is your lock?' She told him what she had done. Then he said: 'Harm has touched me.'"

Some people said: "He only said 'Harm has touched me' when worms reached his heart and tongue, and he feared that they would stop him from remembrance and reflection."

Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr said: "Ayyub had two brothers. They came to him and stood at a distance, unable to come close to him because of his smell. One of them said to his companion: 'If Allah had known any good in Ayyub, He would not have tested him with what we see.'"

He said: "Ayyub never heard anything harder upon him than this word, and he never grieved over anything that befell him as he grieved over that word. At that point he said: 'Harm has touched me.' Then he said: 'O Allah, if You know that I never spent a night full while I knew of a hungry person, then testify for me and bear witness, and they both were listening.' Then he said: 'O Allah, if You know that I never took two shirts at all while I knew of a naked person, then testify for me and bear witness, and they both were listening.' Then he fell down prostrate."

It may be said that its meaning is: "harm touched me" from the gloating of enemies. This is supported by what is related: after he was healed, he was asked, "What was harder on you in your trial?" He said, "The gloating of the enemies."

It is also said: he said that when a worm fell from his thigh, and he picked it up, returned it to its place, and said, "Eat, for God has made me your food." The worm then bit him with a bite whose pain exceeded everything he had suffered from worms' bites.

I heard Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Abiwardi say: I heard Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abbad al-Baghdadi say: Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd was asked about this verse, and he said: "He made him know the need of asking, so that He might bestow upon him the generosity of giving."

I also heard our teacher Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I attended a gathering crowded with jurists and men of letters in the palace of a sultan, and I was asked about this verse. After they had all agreed that Ayyub's saying, "Harm has touched me" (al-Anbiya 21:83), is a complaint, while God the Exalted has said, "Indeed, We found him patient" (Sad 38:44) [p. 44], I said: "This is not a complaint; it is a supplication. Its proof is His words, 'So We answered him' (al-Anbiya 21:84), and answer follows supplication, not complaint." They found this excellent and approved it.

﴿So We removed what harm was upon him, and We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:84). They differed about how this happened. A group said: God the Exalted gave Ayyub in this world the like of his family who had died. As for those who had died, they were not returned to him; rather, God promised Ayyub that He would give them to him in the Hereafter.

'Abd Allah ibn Idris related from Layth, who said: Mujahid sent a man called Qasim to 'Ikrimah to ask him about this verse. He said: It was said to him: "Your family are yours in the Hereafter. If you wish, We will hasten them for you in this world, and if you wish, they will be yours in the Hereafter and We will give you their like in this world." He said: "They will be mine in the Hereafter, and I will be given their like in this world."

He said: He returned to Mujahid and said: He was right. The meaning of the verse according to this interpretation is: "We gave him his family in the Hereafter, and the like of them with them in this world," and by "family" he meant the children.

Wahb said: He had seven daughters and three sons.

Ibn Yasar said: He had seven sons and seven daughters. Others said: rather, God returned them to him in their very persons and gave him their like along with them. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Ka'b, who said: God brought them back to life and he was given their like. This view is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse.

Al-Hasan said: God gave him the like from the offspring of the property that was returned to him and his family; as for the family and property, He returned them to him in their very persons.

﴿As a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:84): an admonition for them. ﴿And Isma'il﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:85), meaning Ibn Ibrahim; ﴿and Idris﴾, who is Enoch; ﴿and Dhu al-Kifl﴾; ﴿each of them was among the patient﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:85), over the command of God. They differed about Dhu al-Kifl.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me by my reading to him in my house, saying: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah [note in the Isfahan copy adds: ibn al-Fadl ibn Fakhurah; Abu Hashim al-Rifa'i said from Ibn Fudayl, al-A'mash said from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah] al-Razi related to us from Sa'd, mawla of Talhah, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ which, if I had heard it only once or twice, I would not have narrated it. I heard it from him more than seven times. He ﷺ said: "There was in the Children of Israel a man called Dhu al-Kifl who did not refrain from any sin he committed. He followed a woman and gave her sixty dinars on condition that she give herself to him. When he sat in the position of a man with a woman, she trembled and wept. He said: 'What makes you weep?' She said: 'Because of this deed; I have never done it before.' He said: 'Did I force you?' She said: 'No, but need compelled me to it.' He said: 'Go, it is yours.' Then he said: 'By God, I will never disobey God again.' He died that very night, and it was said: 'Dhu al-Kifl has died.' They found written on the door of his house: 'Indeed God has forgiven Dhu al-Kifl.'" [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 11/327.]

Al-A'mash related from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, that a prophet of the prophets said: "Who will guarantee for me that he fasts the day, prays the night, and does not become angry?" A young man stood up and said: "I will." He said: "Sit down." Then he returned and said: "Who will guarantee for me that he prays the night, fasts the day, and does not become angry?" That young man stood up and said: "I will." He said: "Sit down." Then he returned, and the young man stood up and said: "I will." He said: "You will pray the night, fast the day, and not become angry?" He said: "Yes."

That prophet died, and that young man sat in his place judging between people, and he never became angry. Then Satan came to him in the form of a man to anger him, while he was fasting and wanted to rest at midday. He struck the door violently, and he said: "Who is this?" He said: "A man with a need." He sent someone with him, and he returned and said: "I am not content with this man." He sent another with him, and he said: "I am not content with this." So he went out to him, took him by the hand, and walked with him until they reached the market, where he left him and departed. Therefore he was named Dhu al-Kifl.

Mujahid said: When al-Yasa' (peace be upon him) grew old, he said: "If only I could appoint a man over the people to govern them during my lifetime, so that I could see how he acts." He gathered the people and said: "Who will undertake for me three things, and I will appoint him: he fasts the day, prays the night, and does not become angry?" A man whom people looked down upon stood up and said: "I will." He dismissed him that day. He said the same thing the next day, and the people remained silent. That man stood up and said: "I will," and he appointed him.

Iblis began saying to the devils: "Get at so-and-so," but they were unable to, so he said: "Leave him to me." He came to him in the form of a poor old man at the time he lay down to rest at midday, for he never slept day or night except that nap. He knocked at the door, and he said: "Who is this?" He said: "A poor old man, great and wronged." So he got up, opened the door, and the man began to recount to him: "There is a dispute between me and my people, and they have wronged me and done so-and-so," and he kept prolonging it until the time of afternoon came and the midday rest was gone. He said: "When you come out in the afternoon, I will take your right for you." So the man went and returned in the afternoon, and he sat in his assembly, looking to see whether he would see the old man, but he did not see him, so he stood up to follow him. The next day he began judging between people while waiting for him, but he did not see him. When he returned to his midday rest and lay down, he came, knocked at the door, and he said: "Who is this?" He said: "The wronged old man." He opened for him, and he said: "Did I not say, when you sit, come to me?" He said: "They are the most treacherous people: when they know you are sitting, they say, 'We will give you your right,' but when you stand, they deny me." He said: "Go, and when you come out in the afternoon, come to me." The midday rest passed him by, so he came out in the afternoon, looked, and did not see him, and sleep overcame him, so he said to some of his household: "Do not let anyone approach this door until I sleep, for sleep has overcome me."

When that hour came, he came, but the man did not give him permission. When he had exhausted his efforts, he looked and saw a window in the house, so he climbed in through it, and behold, he was inside the house, and behold, he was knocking on the door from inside. The man awoke and said: "O so-and-so, did I not order you?" He said: "By God, I was not brought to you from my side. Look, where did I come from?" The man got up to the door, and it was locked as he had locked it, and behold, the man was with him inside the house. He said to him: "Do you sleep while the disputants are at your door?" He recognized him and said: "Are you the enemy of God?" He said: "Yes. You have defeated me in everything, so I did what you see in order to anger you, but God protected you from me." Therefore he was named Dhu al-Kifl, because he undertook a matter and fulfilled it.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: Dhu al-Kifl was not a prophet, but was a righteous servant who undertook the work of a righteous man at his death, and he used to pray to God the Exalted one hundred prayers every day, so God the Mighty and Majestic praised him well.

It is also said: he was a man who undertook the affair of a man who fell into trial, and God saved him through his hands.

It is also said: Dhu al-Kifl was Elias; it is said he was Zechariah. And God knows best.

﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:86). And Dhu al-Nun: mention the companion of the fish, who is Yunus ibn Matta, ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87). They differed about the meaning and interpretation of the verse. Al-Dahhak said: "He went off in anger at his people." This is the report of al-'Awfi and others from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Yunus and his people lived in Palestine. A king invaded them and took captive nine and a half tribes, leaving two and a half tribes. God the Exalted revealed to the prophet Sha'ya: "Go to King Hizqiyah and tell him to send a strong, trustworthy prophet, for I will cast into the hearts of those people that they send with him the Children of Israel." The king said to him: "Whom do you suggest?" In his kingdom there were five prophets, and he said: "Yunus, for he is strong and trustworthy." The king summoned Yunus and ordered him to go out. Yunus said: "Has God commanded you to send me out?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "There are other prophets here who are strong and trustworthy." They insisted upon him, so he went out angry at the prophet, the king, and his people. He came to the Roman Sea, where he found a crowded ship, and he boarded it. When the ship was driven into the deep sea and was tossed until they nearly drowned, the sailors said: "Here is a disobedient man or a runaway slave. Our custom in such cases is to draw lots, and whoever the lot falls upon, we cast into the sea. It is better that one drown than that the ship and all in it be lost." They drew lots three times, and the lot fell upon Yunus each time.

Yunus stood up and said: "I am the disobedient man and the runaway slave," and he threw himself into the water. A fish came and swallowed him; then another fish, larger than it, came and swallowed that fish. God revealed to the fish: "Do not harm a hair of him, for I have made your belly his prison, and I did not make him your food."

Others said: rather, he went away from his people angry at his Lord, when He removed the punishment from them after He had promised it to them. This was because he disliked being among a people who had tested his unreliability regarding what he had promised them, and he was ashamed before them. He did not know the cause by which the punishment and destruction had been averted from them. So he went out angry and said: "By God, I will never return to them as a liar, and I promised them punishment on a day which did not come."

In some reports: it was customary among his people to kill whoever was found to be a liar. When the punishment did not come at the appointed time he had promised them, he feared they would kill him, so he became angry and said: "How can I return to my people when I have broken my promise to them?" He did not know the reason the punishment had been turned away from them, or the manner of the story. He had gone out from among them, and the story has been explained at length in the commentary on Surah Yunus.

Al-Qutayba said: The word al-mughadaba is a form of mufa'alah. The mufa'alah form is mostly from two, as in al-munazara (debating), al-mukhasama (disputing), and al-mujadala (arguing), and it may sometimes be from one, as when you say: "safara" (he traveled), "'aqaba al-rajul" (he punished the man), "tara'aqa al-na'l" (he gave the sandal a ) and "shaarakat al-amr" (he shared the matter), and similar. Here it belongs to this category. So the meaning of His words, mughadaban, is "angry and resentful" (ghadban anifan), and the Arabs call anger "anf" (nose/resentment), and "anf" is anger, because of the closeness of one to the other. Yunus had promised his people that the punishment would come at a fixed term. When the term passed and they were not punished, he became angry and resented returning to them to be called a liar, so he went off like a runaway slave to the ship. From the long suffering and trial he had endured from his people, he wished that God would send down His might upon them.

Al-Hasan [the Basran, per Isfahan copy] said: He was angry at his Lord only because He had commanded him to return to his people to warn them of His might and call them to Him. He asked his Lord to give him respite so that he could prepare to set out to them. It was said to him: "The matter is quicker than that," and he did not wait, but asked to be given time until he could take a sandal to wear. It was said to him something similar to the first saying, and he was a man narrow in temperament, so he said: "My Lord hastened me so that I should take a sandal?" Thus "he went off angry."

Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani said: Yunus ibn Matta was a righteous servant, but he was narrow in temperament. When the burdens of prophethood were laid upon him, he buckled beneath them as a ... buckles under a heavy load, so he threw them from his hand and fled from them. For this reason God the Exalted counted him among those of firm resolve, and He said to His prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): ﴿So be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient﴾ (al-Ahqaf 46:35), and He said: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ (al-Qalam 68:48), meaning: do not meet My command as he met it.

﴿And he thought that We would not decree against him﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87): that We would not impose the punishment upon him. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, and it is the report of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The Arabs say: "qaddara Allah al-shay' bi-qadarihi taqdiran" and "qadara yaqduru qadaran," and from it is His words: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ (al-Waqi'ah 56:60), and His words: ﴿And He who decreed and then guided﴾ (al-A'la 87:3), in the reading of those who lighten them. The evidence for this interpretation is the reading of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Zuhri: "fa-zanna an lan nuqaddira 'alayhi," with a damma on the nun and shaddah on the dal, from taqdir (decreeing). 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and Qatadah read: "fa-zanna an lan yuqaddara 'alayhi," with shaddah in the passive. Ya'qub read "yuqdaru" with lightening in the passive.

A poet said regarding qadar in the sense of taqdir:
"So the evening times of al-Hima will not return to us
forever, as long as the green acacia puts forth leaves.
Nor will return that time which has passed.
Blessed are You; what You decree is benefit, and to You is thanks."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 11/332; the wording there is: "So the evening times of al-Liwa will not return to us forever, as long as the green acacia puts forth leaves."]

'Ata' and many scholars said: its meaning is "fa-zanna an lan nudayyiqa 'alayhi" (he thought that We would not constrict him), from His words: ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:26), that is, He restricts it. And He said: ﴿And whose provision is restricted for him﴾ (al-Talaq 65:7).

Ibn Zayd said: it is an interrogative, meaning: "Did he think that We would not have power over him?"

'Awf related from al-Hasan that he said: its meaning is: "He thought that He would be unable to overpower his Lord, so He could not decree against him."

He said: It has reached me that when Yunus sinned, he set off angry at his Lord, and Satan led him astray until he thought that He would not have power over him.

He said: He had earlier merit and worship, but God refused to leave him to Satan, so He cast him into the belly of the fish. He remained in the belly of the fish for forty days and nights, and it was said: seven days, and it was said: three. God held back his soul and did not kill him there. He repented to his Lord in the belly of the fish and returned to himself, saying: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87), so God brought him out of the belly of the fish by His mercy.

'Awf said: It has reached me that he said: "And I built You a mosque in a place where no one had built one before me." The earlier interpretations are more fitting for the prophets and further from error.

﴿And he called out in the darknesses﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87): that is, the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. This is said by most exegetes. Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd said: the darkness of the belly of the fish, then the darkness of the belly of the other fish that swallowed it in the darkness of the sea.

﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (al-Anbiya 21:87). Muhammad ibn Qays said: Yunus said: "Indeed I have been of the wrongdoers" when I disobeyed You, and in everything I did, I did not worship anyone other than You.

Abu Hurayrah related from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "When God the Exalted willed to imprison Yunus in the belly of the fish, He revealed to the fish: 'Take him, but do not tear his flesh or break his bones.' It took him and then plunged down with him to its dwelling in the sea. When it reached the bottom of the sea, Yunus heard a sound and said to himself: 'What is this?' God revealed to him, while he was in the belly of the fish: 'This is the glorification of the creatures of the sea.' So he glorified God while in the belly of the fish, and the angels heard his glorification and said: 'O our Lord, we hear a faint sound in a strange land!' He said: 'That is My servant Yunus, who disobeyed Me, so I imprisoned him in the belly of the fish.' They said: 'The righteous servant from whom righteous deeds ascended to You every day and night?' He said: 'Yes.' Then they interceded for him, and He commanded the fish, and it cast him onto the shore, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And he was ailing﴾ (al-Saffat 37:145)." [Jami' al-Bayan al-Tabari: 17/107.]

Abu Hilal Muhammad ibn Sulayman related from Shahr ibn Hawshab from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Jibril came to Yunus (peace be upon them both) and said to him: "Go to [the note in the Isfahan copy adds: the people of Nineveh, and warn them that the punishment has drawn near to them]." He said: "Seek a way out." He said: "The matter is quicker than that." He became angry at that and went off to the ship, boarded it, and the ship was held back. They cast lots, and the lot fell upon him. The fish came, wagging its tail, and the fish was called: "We did not make Yunus your provision; We made you a refuge and a mosque for him." The fish swallowed him and carried him from that place until it passed with him by al-Ubulla, then passed with him over the Tigris, then went on until it cast him at Nineveh. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: Yunus's prophethood came only after the fish had spat him out. The evidence for this view is that God mentioned the story of Yunus in Surah al-Saffat, then followed it with His words: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ (al-Saffat 37:147).

Others said: rather, the story of the fish came after his calling his people and delivering to them the message of his Lord, as we have already explained.

Tafsir al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 83–94 (part 4 of 4):

﴿So We responded to him and delivered him from the distress. And thus do We deliver the believers﴾ from their distress when they call out to Us and supplicate Us.

Ali ibn Zayd narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: I heard Sa'd ibn Malik say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The Name of Allah by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked, He gives, is the supplication of Yunus ibn Matta." He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, is it specific to Yunus, or is it for the community of Muslims in general?" He said: "It is specific to Yunus, and general to the believers when they call upon it. Have you not heard the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then he called out in the darknesses﴾ up to His saying ﴿And thus do We deliver the believers﴾? And it is Allah's condition for whoever calls upon Him with it."

The recitation differed regarding His saying "nunji" (﴿nunji﴾). The majority read it with two nuns, the second of them sukun, from al-inja' (deliverance), meaning "We deliver." If it is asked: why was it written in the codices (al-masahif) with one nun? It is answered: because the second nun, when it became sukun and a sukun is not audible on the tongue, was dropped, just as they did with ﴿illa﴾, dropping the nun in ﴿lam-ja'alha﴾ or ﴿kashifa﴾ when it is assimilated into the lam. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, through the narration of Ibn Bakr, read ﴿nunji al-mu'minin﴾ with one nun, a shaddah on the jim, and sukun on the ya'. The grammarians differed regarding this reading. Some of them declared it correct and said: there is an implied element in it, meaning "nunji al-mu'minin," as one says "darab Zayd-an" meaning "darab al-darb Zayd-an" (he struck the striking, Zayd). The poet said:

"Even if a bitch gave birth to a puppy, the puppy would revile the dogs by that [act]."

He meant: it would revile them by that puppy, and it would revile the dogs.

They said: the ya' in "nunji" was made sukun just as they made the ya' sukun in "baqar," saying "baqarah" and similar words. The people of this reading only followed the codex because it is written with one nun.

Al-Qutaybi said: whoever reads with one nun and the shaddah intends "nunji" from al-tanjiyah (rescue), except that he assimilated and dropped one nun seeking lightness.

The grammarians said: this is weak, because the point of articulation of the nun is far from that of the jim. Among those who permitted this reading was Abu 'Ubayd. As for Abu Hatim al-Sijistani, he deemed it a solecism (lahn) and attributed its reader to ignorance, and said: "This is a solecism not permitted in the language, and one may not take such a verse as proof for the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, unless one says: 'wa-kadhalika najji al-mu'minin' (and thus He delivers the believers); and if it were recited thus, it would be correct. And Allah knows best."

﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, saying: "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors"﴾. Zakariyya supplicated his Lord, and said: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan), solitary (wahidan), without a child, without offspring, and grant me an heir." Then he referred the matter to Allah, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and You are the best of inheritors﴾. ﴿So We responded to him and granted him Yahya as a son, and We made his wife fit for him﴾, by making her fertile after she had been barren, as most exegetes said. Some of them said: she had a bad temperament, so He made her fit for him by granting her good character.

﴿Indeed they﴾, meaning the prophets whom He named in this surah,

﴿used to hasten to good deeds, and call upon Us with longing and fear﴾, in fear and hope: longing for the mercy of Allah and fear of the punishment of Allah. Al-A'mash read ﴿rughban wa-ruhban﴾ with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the ghayn and the ha', and both are dialects, like "al-suqm" and "al-suqm," "al-thukl" and "al-thukl," "al-nahl" and "al-nahl," "al-adam" and "al-adam."

﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾, subdued and humble.

﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾, who protected and preserved her private part from what Allah has forbidden. She is Maryam daughter of 'Imran. ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾: We commanded Jibril until he blew into the opening of her garment, and We caused that blowing to become the Messiah in her womb. The Spirit was attributed to Him in the sense of ownership and honour for Maryam and 'Isa, by singling her out with this attribution to Him.

﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾: a proof of the completeness of Our power and wisdom, a woman conceiving without touch of a male, and a child existing without a father. He said "ayatan" (a sign) and did not say "ayatayn" (two signs), because the meaning of the statement is "We made their condition and affair a sign for the worlds."

﴿Indeed this community of yours﴾, your religion, ﴿is one community﴾, one religion, which is Islam; thus He nullified all religions other than Islam. The root of "ummah" is a group that has one single aim, and by the Law it was made one community because its members gather upon one single aim through it. ﴿Ummah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial/absolute element (ʿalā al-qaṭʿ); Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿ummatun﴾ with a nominative, as a repetition (ʿalā al-takrīr).

﴿And I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾. ﴿But they divided their affair﴾ among themselves, meaning they differed in religion and became sects and factions. Then He said: ﴿each to Us they will return﴾, so We will recompense them for their deeds.

﴿So whoever does good deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort﴾: We will not nullify his deed nor deny it, but it will be appreciated and rewarded. ﴿And indeed We are recording it for him﴾: guardians of his deed.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 83–94 (part 1 of 4):

﴿And Ayyub, when he called out to his Lord…﴾ – the verse.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Ayyub was a man from the Romans. He was Ayyub ibn Amus ibn Razih ibn Rum ibn Ays ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and his mother was from the descendants of Lut ibn Haran. Allah the Exalted had chosen him, made him a prophet, and expanded the world for him. He owned the whole of al-Batheniyya in the land of al-Sham, its plains and its mountains with everything in them. He had every kind of wealth, including camels, cattle, horses and donkeys, in a number and abundance that no other man possessed. He had five hundred plough-lands, each worked by five hundred slaves, and each slave had a wife, children and property. Each plough-land yielded a she-ass for him, and each she-ass bore young, two, three, four, five or more. Allah the Exalted had given him a household and children, men and women. He was dutiful and pious, merciful to the poor, a guardian of widows and orphans, generous to guests, and a provider for the wayfarer. He was grateful for the blessings of Allah the Exalted and fulfilled the rights of Allah the Exalted. He was protected from the enemy of Allah, Iblis, so that Iblis could not inflict on him what he inflicts on the wealthy: pride, heedlessness, forgetfulness and being preoccupied with the world to the neglect of the command of Allah. With him were three men who had believed in him, confirmed him and recognised his merit: a man from Yemen called Alyafan, and two men from his land, one called Baldad and the other Safir. They were middle-aged men.

Wahb said: Jibril (peace be upon him) has a station before Allah the Exalted that none of the angels possesses in nearness and excellence. Jibril is the one who receives the speech. When Allah mentions a servant with good, Jibril receives it, then Mika'il receives it from him, and the angels brought near surround the Throne. When this spreads among the angels brought near, the prayer for that servant becomes the prayer of the inhabitants of the heavens. When the angels of the heavens pray for him, they descend with the prayer to the angels of the earth. [[In the Isfahan copy: "From the inhabitants of the heavens the prayer descended upon him to the angels of the earths."]] Iblis, may Allah curse him, was not barred from any of the heavens. He could stand in them wherever he wished, and from there he reached Adam when Allah expelled him from the Garden. He continued to ascend through the heavens until Allah raised Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him), and then he was barred from four of them, though he could still ascend through three. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), he was barred from the remaining three, so he and his armies are barred from all the heavens until the Day of Resurrection, ﴿except one who steals a hearing, and is pursued by a clear flame﴾ [[Al-Hijr: 18.]].

He said: Iblis heard the angels responding with prayer upon Ayyub, at the time when Allah mentioned him and praised him. Envy and resentment overtook him, and he ascended swiftly until he stood at the place in the heaven where he used to stand.
