Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima said: it means its firewood. It is mentioned that *ḥaṣab* in the dialect of the people of Yemen means firewood.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means they will be thrown into the Fire as pebbles are thrown. The root *ḥaṣb* means throwing. It is said: "I pelted the man (*ḥaṣabtu al-rajula*) when I threw at him." Allah, Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed We sent against them a violent wind (ḥāṣiban)﴾, meaning a wind that pelts them with stones. Ibn 'Abbas recited *ḥaḍab* with a ḍād (حَضَبُ), which is everything with which the fire is kindled and fanned. From this the fine sparks of fire are called *ḥaḍab*.

ʿAli and ʿAʾisha recited (the word) with a ṭāʾ, *ḥaṭab* (حَطَبُ), meaning firewood.

A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾.

﴿You will be its (*lahā*) inhabitants (wāridūn)﴾, meaning you will enter it. ﴿If these idols were gods in reality, they would not have entered it﴾, meaning their worshippers would not have entered the Fire; rather, the idols would have protected them. ﴿And each one in it will abide forever﴾, meaning the worshipper and the worshipped.

﴿For them therein is wailing, and they will not hear therein﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said about this verse: When those who will remain forever in the Fire are left in it, they will be placed in coffins of fire. Then these coffins are placed inside other coffins, and those inside still others, and the coffins have nails of fire. They will not hear anything, and no one among them will see that there is anyone else in the Fire being punished.

Then He made an exception, saying, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (reward) has preceded from Us﴾. Some scholars said: *inna* here means *illā* (except), and there is no other instance of this in the Qur'an. *Al-sabq* means one thing preceding another.

﴿For them, from Us, is the best (*al-ḥusnā*)﴾, meaning happiness, the good promise, and the beautiful reward of Paradise. ﴿They will be kept far away from it (mubʿadūn)﴾. *Al-ibʿād* means increasing the distance.

They differed about who these people are. Most exegetes said: they are those who worship something besides Allah while they are obedient to it, and the worship of those who worship it is hateful to them. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the chiefs of Quraysh were in the Ḥaṭīm, around the Kaʿba, and there were three hundred and sixty idols. He sat with them. Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith approached him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) silenced him by argument. Then he recited to him and to them: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, the three verses. Then he stood up. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zabaʿrā ibn Qays ibn ʿAdī al-Sahmī came and saw them whispering. He said: "What is your discussion?" Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to them. ʿAbd Allah said: "By Allah, if I had found him, I would have refuted him." They called the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ibn al-Zabaʿrā said to him: "Did you say: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I have refuted you, by the Lord of the Kaʿba! Do not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes, rather they worship the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then Allah, Glorified, revealed: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾, the verse, meaning ʿUzayr, ʿIsa and the angels.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: By His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, He meant only the idols and not others, because if He had meant the angels and people, He would have said *man taʿbudūna* (who you worship). I say: also because the addressees of this verse are the polytheists of Mecca, and they used to worship idols.

Some of them said: this verse is general for everyone for whom the happiness has preceded from Allah. Muhammad ibn Ḥāṭib said: I heard ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, giving a sermon, and he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom (the best) has preceded﴾, and said: "ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) is among them!"

Al-Junayd said about this verse: "The good fortune (*al-ʿināya*) preceded for them from Allah in the beginning, and the sainthood (*al-wilāya*) appeared in the end."

Abu ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah informed me, saying: Abu al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Nuṣaybī related to us, saying: Abu Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Subaʿī informed us in Aleppo, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār al-Ṣūfī informed us, saying: ʿUbayd Allah al-Qawārīrī related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abi Yazīd al-Hamadhānī related to us, saying: Layth related to us, from the paternal cousin of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, who was among the entertainers (*summār*) of ʿAlī, who said: One night ʿAlī recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us, those will be kept far away from it﴾. He said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf are among them!" Then the prayer was called, and ʿAlī got up, dragging his cloak, saying: ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾, that is, its sound, when they descend to their dwellings in Paradise. ﴿And they will abide forever in that which their souls desire﴾.

*Al-shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure. A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Therein is whatever the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾.

﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Abu Ja'far recited *yaḥzunu* with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy. The others recited it with a fatḥa on the yā' and a ḍamma on the zāy. They differed about *al-faza' al-akbar* (the greatest terror). Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the final blast (*al-nafkha al-ākhira*). The evidence is Allah's saying: ﴿And on the Day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills, and all will come to Him in humility﴾.

Al-Ḥasan said: it is when the servant is commanded to go to the Fire.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is when the Fire closes over the people of the Fire.

Ibn Jurayj said: it is when Death is slaughtered in the form of a white-spotted ram on the Heights, while both groups look on. It will be called out: "O people of Paradise, eternity without death! O people of the Fire, eternity without death!"

Dhu al-Nūn al-Miṣrī said: it is separation, abandonment and parting.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾, meaning they will meet them at the gates of Paradise, congratulating them and saying to them: ﴿This is your day, which you were promised﴾.

﴿On the Day We will roll up the heaven﴾. Abu Ja'far recited *tuṭwā al-samāʾu* (تُطْوَى السَّماءُ) with a ḍamma on the tā' and the hamza, in the passive voice. The others recited it with a nūn, *naṭwī al-samāʾa* (نَطْوِي السَّماءَ), with the accusative on *al-samāʾa*.

﴿Like the rolling up of the scroll for the writings (lil-kutub)﴾. The people of Kufa recited *lil-kutubi* in the plural. Others recited *lil-kitābi* in the singular.

They differed about *al-sijill* (the scroll). Ibn 'Umar and al-Suddī said: *al-sijill* is an angel who writes the deeds of the servants. When it ascends with the seeking of forgiveness, Allah, glorified is He, says: "Write it as light."

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is a sheet (ṣaḥīfa). The *lām* in *lil-kutub* means "upon," according to this interpretation, like folding a sheet over what is written on it.

Abu al-Jawzā' and ʿIkrima related from Ibn ʿAbbās that *al-sijill* is the name of a scribe of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This view is not strong, because the scribes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were well known, and I have mentioned them in my book *al-Rabīʿ*. *Al-sijill* is a noun derived from *al-musājala*, which means mutual writing. Its root is *al-sajl*, which is the bucket. It is said: "I pulled a bucket for the man (*sajjaltu al-rajula*)" when I drew a bucket and he drew a bucket. Then the term was borrowed, and mutual writing and mutual correspondence were called *musājala*. The poet said:

*man yusājilunī yusājil mājidan ... yamlaʾu al-dalwa ilā ʿaqdi al-karab*

"Whoever competes with me in drawing buckets will compete with a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

Then this name was formed on the pattern *faʿl*, like *ṭamr* and *qalz*.

The word *al-ṭayy* (rolling up) in this verse may have two meanings. First, folding, which is the opposite of unfolding, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾.

Second, concealing, obscuring, erasing and effacing, because Allah, glorified is He, will erase its traces and dim its stars, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up, and when the stars fall﴾. The Arabs say: "Conceal (*uṭwi*) this news about so-and-so," meaning hide it and keep it secret.

Then He began a new statement, saying, Mighty is He Who speaks: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾. Most scholars said: just as We began them in the wombs of their mothers, barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, so We will return them on the Day of Resurrection. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, and His saying: ﴿They will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time"﴾.

The evidence for this interpretation is what Layth related from Mujahid, from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me while there was an old woman of the Banu ʿĀmir with me. He said: "Who is this old woman, O ʿĀʾisha?" I said: "One of my maternal aunts." She said: "Ask Allah to admit me to Paradise." He said: "Indeed, Paradise is not entered by old women." The old woman was overcome by distress. He said (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah will create them a creation different from their creation. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed We have created them a (special) creation﴾, the verse." Then he said: "They will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection naked, barefoot and uncircumcised. The first to be clothed will be Ibrahim, peace be upon him."

ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her and with her father, said: "Alas for her shame! Will men not be ashamed before one another?" He said: ﴿For every one of them that Day there will be a matter that will occupy him﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾, like the day his mother bore him.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: He says: "We will destroy everything as it was the first time." It was also said: "As We began it from water, We will return it from dust."

﴿A promise upon Us﴾. It is in the accusative as an infinitive (*maṣdar*), meaning: "We promised it, a promise upon Us." ﴿Indeed We are ever doing it﴾, meaning the return and the resurrection.

﴿And We had already written in the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*) after the Reminder (*al-dhikr*)﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza recited *al-Zubūri* with a ḍamma on the zāy. The others recite it with a fatḥa, and it means *al-mazbūr* (the written), like *al-ḥalūb* and *al-rukūb*. It is said: "I wrote the book (*zabartu al-kitāba*) and *dhabartuhu*" when I wrote it.

They differed about the meaning of *al-zabūr* in this verse. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: by *al-zabūr* is meant the revealed books, and by *al-dhikr* (the Reminder) is meant the Mother of the Book, which is with Him.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *al-dhikr* is the Torah, and *al-zabūr* refers to the revealed books after the Torah.

Al-Shaʿbī said: *al-Zabūr* is the book of Dawud (David), and *al-dhikr* is the Torah.

Some scholars said: "The Zabur is the Zabur of Dawud (David), and the Dhikr is the Qur'an." "Ba'd" here means "qabl" (before), as in His saying: ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾ [Surah al-Kahf 18:79], meaning "in front of them." And His saying: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [Surah al-Nazi'at 79:30], meaning "before that."

﴿That the earth﴾ means the land of Paradise. ﴿My righteous servants shall inherit it﴾ means the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is the view of Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliyah. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the earth"﴾ [Surah al-Zumar 39:74].

Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant that the earth in this world will become the possession of the believers. This is a ruling from Allah, the Exalted, of the manifestation of the religion, the strengthening of the Muslims, and the subjugation of the disbelievers.

Wahb said: "I read in several of the books of Allah that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Indeed I shall cause to inherit the earth My righteous servants from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).'"

﴿Indeed, in this is a message﴾ meaning a means of reaching the desired goal. Whoever follows the Qur'an and acts upon it reaches what he hopes for in reward. Thus the Qur'an is the provision for Paradise, like the provision of a traveller.

﴿For a people who worship﴾ meaning believers who worship Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "[It means] those who have knowledge." Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "They are the community of Muhammad, the people of the five prayers and of the month of Ramadan; Allah, the Exalted, named them 'worshippers'."

﴿And We have not sent you, O Muhammad, except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ Ibn Zayd said: "It means the believers specifically." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is general: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, mercy is written for him in this world and the Hereafter; and whoever does not believe is spared from what befell the nations of transformation, sinking into the earth, and hurling of stones."

﴿Say, "It is only revealed to me that your god is one God; so will you submit?" And if they turn away, say, "I have announced to you on equal terms,"﴾ meaning: I have informed you clearly that between me and you there is war and no peace, and that I oppose your religion. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿on equal terms﴾ is that in the warning I have not favoured some of you with something I concealed from others. And it was said: that you may be equal in belief in it. This is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an.

﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ meaning the Resurrection. It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya' 21:97 in some readings; cf. commentary].

﴿Indeed, He knows what is said openly and knows what you conceal. And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾ "Perhaps" here means: perhaps the delay of punishment from you is a trial for you, a test, to see how you act, though He is more knowing. ﴿And provision for a time﴾ means until a term at which Allah decides what He wills.

Abu Bakr al-Juzqi informed us: Abu al-'Abbas al-Da'uli informed us: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Khaythamah informed us: Muhammad ibn Abi Ghalib informed us: Hisham informed us: Mujalid informed us: al-Sab'i informed me: When al-Hasan ibn 'Ali handed over the affair to Mu'awiyah, Mu'awiyah said to him, "Stand up, deliver a sermon, and apologise to the people." Al-Hasan stood and gave a sermon; he praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "Indeed the shrewdest of the shrewd is piety, and the most foolish of foolishness is immorality. And this matter over which I and Mu'awiyah disagreed is either the right of a man who had more right to it, or a right that was mine which I left, seeking the reconciliation of this community." Then he said: ﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾

﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ That is: "Decide between me and those who denied me with truth." Allah does not judge except with truth. There are two interpretations regarding it:

The people of exegesis said: "The truth here means the punishment, as though he sought punishment quickly for his people, and they were punished on the day of Badr and its night." A parallel is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 7:89].

Qatadah said: "When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) witnessed battle, he would say: 'My Lord, judge with truth.'"

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the meaning is "My Lord, judge by Your true judgment," so the word "judgment" is omitted and "truth" is put in its place.

The readers differed concerning this verse. Hafs read ﴿Qala﴾ with an alif, as a statement. The rest read "Qul" as a command. Abu Ja'far read "Rabbu" with a damma on the ba' as a vocative and a definite noun. al-Dahhak and Ya'qub read "Rabbi uhkum" with the yā' affirmed, in the sense of a statement that Allah is the most just of all judges; this reading is not accepted because it contradicts the codex (mushaf). The remaining readers read ﴿Rabbi uhkum﴾ as a supplication.

﴿And our Lord, the Most Merciful, is the One sought for help against what you describe.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 95–112 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And forbidden is (for) a town﴾. The people of Kufa recited *wa-ḥimrun* (وَحِرْمٌ) with a kasra on the ḥa' and a sukun on the ra', without an alif. The others recited *wa-ḥarāmun* (وَحَرامٌ). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Ḥatim preferred this second reading. Both are dialectal variants, like *ḥill* and *ḥalāl*.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of the verse, ﴿And forbidden is (for) a town whom We have destroyed﴾, is that its people will not return after destruction. According to this interpretation, the *lā* (لا) is extra (*ṣila*), as in the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

*fī sirrin lā ḥūrā sarā wa-mā shaʿar*

meaning: "in a well, not ... he travelled by night and did not perceive," that is, "in a well of ḥūr."

Others said: *al-ḥarām* here means *al-wājib* (obligatory), as in the verse of al-Khansa':

*wa-inna ḥarāman lā arā al-dahra bākiyan ʿalā shajwihi illā bakaytu ʿalā ʿAmr*

"Indeed, it is obligatory that I never see anyone weeping over his grief through time except that I weep over ʿAmr." According to this interpretation, *lā* is an affirmative particle (*thābit*).

Jabir al-Ju'fi said: I asked Abu Ja'far about the return (*al-raj'a*), and he recited this verse.

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾. The majority recited *futiḥat* (فُتِحَتْ) with light emphasis. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub recited it with emphasis, *futtiḥat* (فُتِّحَتْ), on the kasra. The meaning of the verse is that the barrier is opened for Gog and Magog (*Yājūj wa-Mājūj*). We have already explained their story in the commentary.

Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir related from Rib'i ibn Khirash, from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first of the signs are the Dajjal (the Antichrist), the descent of ʿIsa (Jesus), a fire that comes out of the bottom of Aden in Yemen and drives people toward the place of assembly, staying with them at night when they rest, the smoke, the beast (*al-dābba*), and then Gog and Magog."

Ḥudhayfa said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what are Gog and Magog?" He said: "They are nations. Each nation is four hundred thousand nations. A man among them does not die until he sees a thousand eyes blinking before him from his own loins. They are the children of Adam (peace be upon him). They march toward the ruin of the world. Their vanguard will be in Syria and their rear in Iraq. They pass by the rivers of the world and drink the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Sea of Tiberias, until they come to Jerusalem. They say, 'We have killed the people of the world,' so they fight whoever is in the heaven. They shoot arrows toward the sky, and their arrows return to them stained with blood, and they say, 'We have killed those in the heaven.'"

ʿIsa and the Muslims are at the Mount of Sinai (*Ṭūr Sīnīn*). Allah, glorified is He, reveals to ʿIsa: "Take My servants into the mountain and what is near it." Then ʿIsa raises his hands to the sky, and the Muslims say, "Amen." Allah sends upon them a worm called *al-Naghf* (in the copy of Isfahan: *al-ʿArf*), which enters their nostrils. They become dead from the farthest part of Syria to the farthest part of the East (in Tafsir al-Tabari: Iraq; in the copy of Isfahan: the West), until the earth stinks from their corpses. Allah commands the sky, and it rains like the mouths of waterskins, washing the earth of their corpses and stench. At that time, the sun rises from the west."

﴿And they, from every hill (ḥadab), are swarming﴾. *Ḥadab* means a rise and a hill. *Yanselūn* means they come out walking swiftly, like the rapid gait of a wolf.

The scholars differed about this pronoun. One group said it refers to Gog and Magog, and they cited the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Gog and Magog will be let loose, and they will come out upon the people, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿from every hill they swarm﴾, and they will overrun the earth."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), regarding what is mentioned about ʿIsa, who said: "ʿIsa said: My Lord has commanded me that the Dajjal will come out, and that I will descend to him. It is mentioned that he has two canes. When he sees me, Allah will destroy him." He said: "He will melt as lead melts, until even the tree and the stone will say, 'O Muslim, this is a disbeliever, so kill him.' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will destroy them, and people will return to their lands and homelands. Then Gog and Magog will come to them ﴿from every hill swarming﴾. They will not pass over anything without destroying it, and they will not pass over water without drinking it."

Others said: the pronoun refers to all creation, meaning that they will come out of their graves and places and be gathered to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. This is supported by Mujahid's recitation, *wa-hum min kulli jadathin* (وَهُمْ مِنْ كُلِّ جَدَثٍ), with a jim and a tha', meaning the grave, based on Allah's saying: ﴿So, when they come out from the graves to their Lord, they swarm﴾.

﴿And the true promise draws near﴾, meaning the Resurrection. Al-Farra' (a grammarian) and a group of scholars said: the *wāw* in ﴿and draws near﴾ is superfluous (*muqḥam*), and the meaning of the verse is: "Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, the true promise draws near." A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿So when they both had submitted, and he had laid him down upon his forehead, and We called out to him﴾, meaning "We called out to him." Imru' al-Qays said:

*fa-lammā ajznā sāḥata al-ḥayyi wa-ntaḥā bi-bāṭini khabtin dhī qifāfin ʿaqanqali*

"When we passed the open area of the tribe and he turned aside into the bottom of a valley with ridges and winding sand hills," meaning *intaḥā* (he turned aside). The evidence for this interpretation is the hadith of Ḥudhayfa, who said: "If a man kept a colt after the emergence of Gog and Magog, he would not ride it until the Hour is established."

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian) said: The Basrans do not permit omitting the *wāw*, and they make the answer of *ḥattā idhā futiḥat* (until, when ... are opened) to be ﴿They say: O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾. The verse would then be: ﴿until, when Gog and Magog are let loose ... and the true promise draws near, they say: O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾.

﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾. In the phrase ﴿it﴾ (*hiya*) there are three possibilities:

First, *hiya* may refer to *al-abṣār* (the eyes), and *al-abṣār* (the eyes) that follows may be an explanation of it, as in the verse of a poet:

*la-ʿamru abīhā lā taqūlu ẓaʿīnatī ... alā firra ʿannī mālikun ibnu Abī Kaʿbi*

"By the life of her father, my she-camel does not say, 'Ah, flee from me, Malik ibn Abi Kaʿb.'" Here the poet refers to the camel (*ẓaʿīna*) by the pronoun in *abīhā* and then makes it explicit. So the meaning of the statement is: "Then, the eyes are staring fixedly, the eyes of those who disbelieved."

Second, *hiya* may be a dummy pronoun (*ʿimād*), as in Allah's saying: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind﴾, and as in the verse of a poet: "So is it raised by what is here, a head?"

Third, the sentence may end at *hiya*, meaning "it is present, standing," that is, it is so near that it is as if it is coming and present. Then a new sentence begins: *shākhiṣatun abṣāru alladhīna kafarū* (the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring fixedly), with the predicate placed before the subject. The meaning is: the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring fixedly from the terror of the Hour's standing. They say: ﴿O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾, that is, of this day. ﴿Nay, we were wrongdoers﴾, by disobeying our Lord and placing worship in other than its proper place.

﴿Indeed you, O polytheists, and what you worship besides Allah﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿are fuel (ḥaṣab) for Hell﴾. The common recitation is with a ṣād (حَصَبُ). It means its fuel, according to Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima said: it means its firewood. It is mentioned that *ḥaṣab* in the dialect of the people of Yemen means firewood.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means they will be thrown into the Fire as pebbles are thrown. The root *ḥaṣb* means throwing. It is said: "I pelted the man (*ḥaṣabtu al-rajula*) when I threw at him." Allah, Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed We sent against them a violent wind (ḥāṣiban)﴾, meaning a wind that pelts them with stones. Ibn 'Abbas recited *ḥaḍab* with a ḍād (حَضَبُ), which is everything with which the fire is kindled and fanned. From this the fine sparks of fire are called *ḥaḍab*.

ʿAli and ʿAʾisha recited (the word) with a ṭāʾ, *ḥaṭab* (حَطَبُ), meaning firewood.

A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾.

﴿You will be its (*lahā*) inhabitants (wāridūn)﴾, meaning you will enter it. ﴿If these idols were gods in reality, they would not have entered it﴾, meaning their worshippers would not have entered the Fire; rather, the idols would have protected them. ﴿And each one in it will abide forever﴾, meaning the worshipper and the worshipped.

﴿For them therein is wailing, and they will not hear therein﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said about this verse: When those who will remain forever in the Fire are left in it, they will be placed in coffins of fire. Then these coffins are placed inside other coffins, and those inside still others, and the coffins have nails of fire. They will not hear anything, and no one among them will see that there is anyone else in the Fire being punished.

Then He made an exception, saying, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (reward) has preceded from Us﴾. Some scholars said: *inna* here means *illā* (except), and there is no other instance of this in the Qur'an. *Al-sabq* means one thing preceding another.

﴿For them, from Us, is the best (*al-ḥusnā*)﴾, meaning happiness, the good promise, and the beautiful reward of Paradise. ﴿They will be kept far away from it (mubʿadūn)﴾. *Al-ibʿād* means increasing the distance.

They differed about who these people are. Most exegetes said: they are those who worship something besides Allah while they are obedient to it, and the worship of those who worship it is hateful to them. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the chiefs of Quraysh were in the Ḥaṭīm, around the Kaʿba, and there were three hundred and sixty idols. He sat with them. Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith approached him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) silenced him by argument. Then he recited to him and to them: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, the three verses. Then he stood up. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zabaʿrā ibn Qays ibn ʿAdī al-Sahmī came and saw them whispering. He said: "What is your discussion?" Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to them. ʿAbd Allah said: "By Allah, if I had found him, I would have refuted him." They called the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ibn al-Zabaʿrā said to him: "Did you say: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I have refuted you, by the Lord of the Kaʿba! Do not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes, rather they worship the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then Allah, Glorified, revealed: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾, the verse, meaning ʿUzayr, ʿIsa and the angels.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: By His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, He meant only the idols and not others, because if He had meant the angels and people, He would have said *man taʿbudūna* (who you worship). I say: also because the addressees of this verse are the polytheists of Mecca, and they used to worship idols.

Some of them said: this verse is general for everyone for whom the happiness has preceded from Allah. Muhammad ibn Ḥāṭib said: I heard ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, giving a sermon, and he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom (the best) has preceded﴾, and said: "ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) is among them!"

Al-Junayd said about this verse: "The good fortune (*al-ʿināya*) preceded for them from Allah in the beginning, and the sainthood (*al-wilāya*) appeared in the end."

Abu ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah informed me, saying: Abu al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Nuṣaybī related to us, saying: Abu Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Subaʿī informed us in Aleppo, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār al-Ṣūfī informed us, saying: ʿUbayd Allah al-Qawārīrī related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abi Yazīd al-Hamadhānī related to us, saying: Layth related to us, from the paternal cousin of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, who was among the entertainers (*summār*) of ʿAlī, who said: One night ʿAlī recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us, those will be kept far away from it﴾. He said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf are among them!" Then the prayer was called, and ʿAlī got up, dragging his cloak, saying: ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾, that is, its sound, when they descend to their dwellings in Paradise. ﴿And they will abide forever in that which their souls desire﴾.

*Al-shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure. A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Therein is whatever the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾.

﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Abu Ja'far recited *yaḥzunu* with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy. The others recited it with a fatḥa on the yā' and a ḍamma on the zāy. They differed about *al-faza' al-akbar* (the greatest terror). Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the final blast (*al-nafkha al-ākhira*). The evidence is Allah's saying: ﴿And on the Day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills, and all will come to Him in humility﴾.

Al-Ḥasan said: it is when the servant is commanded to go to the Fire.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is when the Fire closes over the people of the Fire.

Ibn Jurayj said: it is when Death is slaughtered in the form of a white-spotted ram on the Heights, while both groups look on. It will be called out: "O people of Paradise, eternity without death! O people of the Fire, eternity without death!"

Dhu al-Nūn al-Miṣrī said: it is separation, abandonment and parting.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾, meaning they will meet them at the gates of Paradise, congratulating them and saying to them: ﴿This is your day, which you were promised﴾.

﴿On the Day We will roll up the heaven﴾. Abu Ja'far recited *tuṭwā al-samāʾu* (تُطْوَى السَّماءُ) with a ḍamma on the tā' and the hamza, in the passive voice. The others recited it with a nūn, *naṭwī al-samāʾa* (نَطْوِي السَّماءَ), with the accusative on *al-samāʾa*.

﴿Like the rolling up of the scroll for the writings (lil-kutub)﴾. The people of Kufa recited *lil-kutubi* in the plural. Others recited *lil-kitābi* in the singular.

They differed about *al-sijill* (the scroll). Ibn 'Umar and al-Suddī said: *al-sijill* is an angel who writes the deeds of the servants. When it ascends with the seeking of forgiveness, Allah, glorified is He, says: "Write it as light."

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is a sheet (ṣaḥīfa). The *lām* in *lil-kutub* means "upon," according to this interpretation, like folding a sheet over what is written on it.

Abu al-Jawzā' and ʿIkrima related from Ibn ʿAbbās that *al-sijill* is the name of a scribe of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This view is not strong, because the scribes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were well known, and I have mentioned them in my book *al-Rabīʿ*. *Al-sijill* is a noun derived from *al-musājala*, which means mutual writing. Its root is *al-sajl*, which is the bucket. It is said: "I pulled a bucket for the man (*sajjaltu al-rajula*)" when I drew a bucket and he drew a bucket. Then the term was borrowed, and mutual writing and mutual correspondence were called *musājala*. The poet said:

*man yusājilunī yusājil mājidan ... yamlaʾu al-dalwa ilā ʿaqdi al-karab*

"Whoever competes with me in drawing buckets will compete with a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

Then this name was formed on the pattern *faʿl*, like *ṭamr* and *qalz*.

The word *al-ṭayy* (rolling up) in this verse may have two meanings. First, folding, which is the opposite of unfolding, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾.

Second, concealing, obscuring, erasing and effacing, because Allah, glorified is He, will erase its traces and dim its stars, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up, and when the stars fall﴾. The Arabs say: "Conceal (*uṭwi*) this news about so-and-so," meaning hide it and keep it secret.

Then He began a new statement, saying, Mighty is He Who speaks: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾. Most scholars said: just as We began them in the wombs of their mothers, barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, so We will return them on the Day of Resurrection. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, and His saying: ﴿They will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time"﴾.

The evidence for this interpretation is what Layth related from Mujahid, from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me while there was an old woman of the Banu ʿĀmir with me. He said: "Who is this old woman, O ʿĀʾisha?" I said: "One of my maternal aunts." She said: "Ask Allah to admit me to Paradise." He said: "Indeed, Paradise is not entered by old women." The old woman was overcome by distress. He said (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah will create them a creation different from their creation. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed We have created them a (special) creation﴾, the verse." Then he said: "They will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection naked, barefoot and uncircumcised. The first to be clothed will be Ibrahim, peace be upon him."

ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her and with her father, said: "Alas for her shame! Will men not be ashamed before one another?" He said: ﴿For every one of them that Day there will be a matter that will occupy him﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾, like the day his mother bore him.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: He says: "We will destroy everything as it was the first time." It was also said: "As We began it from water, We will return it from dust."

﴿A promise upon Us﴾. It is in the accusative as an infinitive (*maṣdar*), meaning: "We promised it, a promise upon Us." ﴿Indeed We are ever doing it﴾, meaning the return and the resurrection.

﴿And We had already written in the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*) after the Reminder (*al-dhikr*)﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza recited *al-Zubūri* with a ḍamma on the zāy. The others recite it with a fatḥa, and it means *al-mazbūr* (the written), like *al-ḥalūb* and *al-rukūb*. It is said: "I wrote the book (*zabartu al-kitāba*) and *dhabartuhu*" when I wrote it.

They differed about the meaning of *al-zabūr* in this verse. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: by *al-zabūr* is meant the revealed books, and by *al-dhikr* (the Reminder) is meant the Mother of the Book, which is with Him.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *al-dhikr* is the Torah, and *al-zabūr* refers to the revealed books after the Torah.

Al-Shaʿbī said: *al-Zabūr* is the book of Dawud (David), and *al-dhikr* is the Torah.

Some scholars said: "The Zabur is the Zabur of Dawud (David), and the Dhikr is the Qur'an." "Ba'd" here means "qabl" (before), as in His saying: ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾ [Surah al-Kahf 18:79], meaning "in front of them." And His saying: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [Surah al-Nazi'at 79:30], meaning "before that."

﴿That the earth﴾ means the land of Paradise. ﴿My righteous servants shall inherit it﴾ means the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is the view of Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliyah. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the earth"﴾ [Surah al-Zumar 39:74].

Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant that the earth in this world will become the possession of the believers. This is a ruling from Allah, the Exalted, of the manifestation of the religion, the strengthening of the Muslims, and the subjugation of the disbelievers.

Wahb said: "I read in several of the books of Allah that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Indeed I shall cause to inherit the earth My righteous servants from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).'"

﴿Indeed, in this is a message﴾ meaning a means of reaching the desired goal. Whoever follows the Qur'an and acts upon it reaches what he hopes for in reward. Thus the Qur'an is the provision for Paradise, like the provision of a traveller.

﴿For a people who worship﴾ meaning believers who worship Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "[It means] those who have knowledge." Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "They are the community of Muhammad, the people of the five prayers and of the month of Ramadan; Allah, the Exalted, named them 'worshippers'."

﴿And We have not sent you, O Muhammad, except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ Ibn Zayd said: "It means the believers specifically." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is general: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, mercy is written for him in this world and the Hereafter; and whoever does not believe is spared from what befell the nations of transformation, sinking into the earth, and hurling of stones."

﴿Say, "It is only revealed to me that your god is one God; so will you submit?" And if they turn away, say, "I have announced to you on equal terms,"﴾ meaning: I have informed you clearly that between me and you there is war and no peace, and that I oppose your religion. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿on equal terms﴾ is that in the warning I have not favoured some of you with something I concealed from others. And it was said: that you may be equal in belief in it. This is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an.

﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ meaning the Resurrection. It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya' 21:97 in some readings; cf. commentary].

﴿Indeed, He knows what is said openly and knows what you conceal. And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾ "Perhaps" here means: perhaps the delay of punishment from you is a trial for you, a test, to see how you act, though He is more knowing. ﴿And provision for a time﴾ means until a term at which Allah decides what He wills.

Abu Bakr al-Juzqi informed us: Abu al-'Abbas al-Da'uli informed us: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Khaythamah informed us: Muhammad ibn Abi Ghalib informed us: Hisham informed us: Mujalid informed us: al-Sab'i informed me: When al-Hasan ibn 'Ali handed over the affair to Mu'awiyah, Mu'awiyah said to him, "Stand up, deliver a sermon, and apologise to the people." Al-Hasan stood and gave a sermon; he praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "Indeed the shrewdest of the shrewd is piety, and the most foolish of foolishness is immorality. And this matter over which I and Mu'awiyah disagreed is either the right of a man who had more right to it, or a right that was mine which I left, seeking the reconciliation of this community." Then he said: ﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾

﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ That is: "Decide between me and those who denied me with truth." Allah does not judge except with truth. There are two interpretations regarding it:

The people of exegesis said: "The truth here means the punishment, as though he sought punishment quickly for his people, and they were punished on the day of Badr and its night." A parallel is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 7:89].

Qatadah said: "When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) witnessed battle, he would say: 'My Lord, judge with truth.'"

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the meaning is "My Lord, judge by Your true judgment," so the word "judgment" is omitted and "truth" is put in its place.

The readers differed concerning this verse. Hafs read ﴿Qala﴾ with an alif, as a statement. The rest read "Qul" as a command. Abu Ja'far read "Rabbu" with a damma on the ba' as a vocative and a definite noun. al-Dahhak and Ya'qub read "Rabbi uhkum" with the yā' affirmed, in the sense of a statement that Allah is the most just of all judges; this reading is not accepted because it contradicts the codex (mushaf). The remaining readers read ﴿Rabbi uhkum﴾ as a supplication.

﴿And our Lord, the Most Merciful, is the One sought for help against what you describe.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 95–112 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And forbidden is (for) a town﴾. The people of Kufa recited *wa-ḥimrun* (وَحِرْمٌ) with a kasra on the ḥa' and a sukun on the ra', without an alif. The others recited *wa-ḥarāmun* (وَحَرامٌ). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Ḥatim preferred this second reading. Both are dialectal variants, like *ḥill* and *ḥalāl*.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of the verse, ﴿And forbidden is (for) a town whom We have destroyed﴾, is that its people will not return after destruction. According to this interpretation, the *lā* (لا) is extra (*ṣila*), as in the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

*fī sirrin lā ḥūrā sarā wa-mā shaʿar*

meaning: "in a well, not ... he travelled by night and did not perceive," that is, "in a well of ḥūr."

Others said: *al-ḥarām* here means *al-wājib* (obligatory), as in the verse of al-Khansa':

*wa-inna ḥarāman lā arā al-dahra bākiyan ʿalā shajwihi illā bakaytu ʿalā ʿAmr*

"Indeed, it is obligatory that I never see anyone weeping over his grief through time except that I weep over ʿAmr." According to this interpretation, *lā* is an affirmative particle (*thābit*).

Jabir al-Ju'fi said: I asked Abu Ja'far about the return (*al-raj'a*), and he recited this verse.

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾. The majority recited *futiḥat* (فُتِحَتْ) with light emphasis. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub recited it with emphasis, *futtiḥat* (فُتِّحَتْ), on the kasra. The meaning of the verse is that the barrier is opened for Gog and Magog (*Yājūj wa-Mājūj*). We have already explained their story in the commentary.

Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir related from Rib'i ibn Khirash, from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first of the signs are the Dajjal (the Antichrist), the descent of ʿIsa (Jesus), a fire that comes out of the bottom of Aden in Yemen and drives people toward the place of assembly, staying with them at night when they rest, the smoke, the beast (*al-dābba*), and then Gog and Magog."

Ḥudhayfa said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what are Gog and Magog?" He said: "They are nations. Each nation is four hundred thousand nations. A man among them does not die until he sees a thousand eyes blinking before him from his own loins. They are the children of Adam (peace be upon him). They march toward the ruin of the world. Their vanguard will be in Syria and their rear in Iraq. They pass by the rivers of the world and drink the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Sea of Tiberias, until they come to Jerusalem. They say, 'We have killed the people of the world,' so they fight whoever is in the heaven. They shoot arrows toward the sky, and their arrows return to them stained with blood, and they say, 'We have killed those in the heaven.'"

ʿIsa and the Muslims are at the Mount of Sinai (*Ṭūr Sīnīn*). Allah, glorified is He, reveals to ʿIsa: "Take My servants into the mountain and what is near it." Then ʿIsa raises his hands to the sky, and the Muslims say, "Amen." Allah sends upon them a worm called *al-Naghf* (in the copy of Isfahan: *al-ʿArf*), which enters their nostrils. They become dead from the farthest part of Syria to the farthest part of the East (in Tafsir al-Tabari: Iraq; in the copy of Isfahan: the West), until the earth stinks from their corpses. Allah commands the sky, and it rains like the mouths of waterskins, washing the earth of their corpses and stench. At that time, the sun rises from the west."

﴿And they, from every hill (ḥadab), are swarming﴾. *Ḥadab* means a rise and a hill. *Yanselūn* means they come out walking swiftly, like the rapid gait of a wolf.

The scholars differed about this pronoun. One group said it refers to Gog and Magog, and they cited the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Gog and Magog will be let loose, and they will come out upon the people, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿from every hill they swarm﴾, and they will overrun the earth."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), regarding what is mentioned about ʿIsa, who said: "ʿIsa said: My Lord has commanded me that the Dajjal will come out, and that I will descend to him. It is mentioned that he has two canes. When he sees me, Allah will destroy him." He said: "He will melt as lead melts, until even the tree and the stone will say, 'O Muslim, this is a disbeliever, so kill him.' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will destroy them, and people will return to their lands and homelands. Then Gog and Magog will come to them ﴿from every hill swarming﴾. They will not pass over anything without destroying it, and they will not pass over water without drinking it."

Others said: the pronoun refers to all creation, meaning that they will come out of their graves and places and be gathered to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. This is supported by Mujahid's recitation, *wa-hum min kulli jadathin* (وَهُمْ مِنْ كُلِّ جَدَثٍ), with a jim and a tha', meaning the grave, based on Allah's saying: ﴿So, when they come out from the graves to their Lord, they swarm﴾.

﴿And the true promise draws near﴾, meaning the Resurrection. Al-Farra' (a grammarian) and a group of scholars said: the *wāw* in ﴿and draws near﴾ is superfluous (*muqḥam*), and the meaning of the verse is: "Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, the true promise draws near." A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿So when they both had submitted, and he had laid him down upon his forehead, and We called out to him﴾, meaning "We called out to him." Imru' al-Qays said:

*fa-lammā ajznā sāḥata al-ḥayyi wa-ntaḥā bi-bāṭini khabtin dhī qifāfin ʿaqanqali*

"When we passed the open area of the tribe and he turned aside into the bottom of a valley with ridges and winding sand hills," meaning *intaḥā* (he turned aside). The evidence for this interpretation is the hadith of Ḥudhayfa, who said: "If a man kept a colt after the emergence of Gog and Magog, he would not ride it until the Hour is established."

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian) said: The Basrans do not permit omitting the *wāw*, and they make the answer of *ḥattā idhā futiḥat* (until, when ... are opened) to be ﴿They say: O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾. The verse would then be: ﴿until, when Gog and Magog are let loose ... and the true promise draws near, they say: O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾.

﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾. In the phrase ﴿it﴾ (*hiya*) there are three possibilities:

First, *hiya* may refer to *al-abṣār* (the eyes), and *al-abṣār* (the eyes) that follows may be an explanation of it, as in the verse of a poet:

*la-ʿamru abīhā lā taqūlu ẓaʿīnatī ... alā firra ʿannī mālikun ibnu Abī Kaʿbi*

"By the life of her father, my she-camel does not say, 'Ah, flee from me, Malik ibn Abi Kaʿb.'" Here the poet refers to the camel (*ẓaʿīna*) by the pronoun in *abīhā* and then makes it explicit. So the meaning of the statement is: "Then, the eyes are staring fixedly, the eyes of those who disbelieved."

Second, *hiya* may be a dummy pronoun (*ʿimād*), as in Allah's saying: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind﴾, and as in the verse of a poet: "So is it raised by what is here, a head?"

Third, the sentence may end at *hiya*, meaning "it is present, standing," that is, it is so near that it is as if it is coming and present. Then a new sentence begins: *shākhiṣatun abṣāru alladhīna kafarū* (the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring fixedly), with the predicate placed before the subject. The meaning is: the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring fixedly from the terror of the Hour's standing. They say: ﴿O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾, that is, of this day. ﴿Nay, we were wrongdoers﴾, by disobeying our Lord and placing worship in other than its proper place.

﴿Indeed you, O polytheists, and what you worship besides Allah﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿are fuel (ḥaṣab) for Hell﴾. The common recitation is with a ṣād (حَصَبُ). It means its fuel, according to Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima said: it means its firewood. It is mentioned that *ḥaṣab* in the dialect of the people of Yemen means firewood.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means they will be thrown into the Fire as pebbles are thrown. The root *ḥaṣb* means throwing. It is said: "I pelted the man (*ḥaṣabtu al-rajula*) when I threw at him." Allah, Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed We sent against them a violent wind (ḥāṣiban)﴾, meaning a wind that pelts them with stones. Ibn 'Abbas recited *ḥaḍab* with a ḍād (حَضَبُ), which is everything with which the fire is kindled and fanned. From this the fine sparks of fire are called *ḥaḍab*.

ʿAli and ʿAʾisha recited (the word) with a ṭāʾ, *ḥaṭab* (حَطَبُ), meaning firewood.

A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾.

﴿You will be its (*lahā*) inhabitants (wāridūn)﴾, meaning you will enter it. ﴿If these idols were gods in reality, they would not have entered it﴾, meaning their worshippers would not have entered the Fire; rather, the idols would have protected them. ﴿And each one in it will abide forever﴾, meaning the worshipper and the worshipped.

﴿For them therein is wailing, and they will not hear therein﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said about this verse: When those who will remain forever in the Fire are left in it, they will be placed in coffins of fire. Then these coffins are placed inside other coffins, and those inside still others, and the coffins have nails of fire. They will not hear anything, and no one among them will see that there is anyone else in the Fire being punished.

Then He made an exception, saying, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (reward) has preceded from Us﴾. Some scholars said: *inna* here means *illā* (except), and there is no other instance of this in the Qur'an. *Al-sabq* means one thing preceding another.

﴿For them, from Us, is the best (*al-ḥusnā*)﴾, meaning happiness, the good promise, and the beautiful reward of Paradise. ﴿They will be kept far away from it (mubʿadūn)﴾. *Al-ibʿād* means increasing the distance.

They differed about who these people are. Most exegetes said: they are those who worship something besides Allah while they are obedient to it, and the worship of those who worship it is hateful to them. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the chiefs of Quraysh were in the Ḥaṭīm, around the Kaʿba, and there were three hundred and sixty idols. He sat with them. Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith approached him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) silenced him by argument. Then he recited to him and to them: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, the three verses. Then he stood up. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zabaʿrā ibn Qays ibn ʿAdī al-Sahmī came and saw them whispering. He said: "What is your discussion?" Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to them. ʿAbd Allah said: "By Allah, if I had found him, I would have refuted him." They called the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ibn al-Zabaʿrā said to him: "Did you say: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I have refuted you, by the Lord of the Kaʿba! Do not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes, rather they worship the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then Allah, Glorified, revealed: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾, the verse, meaning ʿUzayr, ʿIsa and the angels.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: By His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, He meant only the idols and not others, because if He had meant the angels and people, He would have said *man taʿbudūna* (who you worship). I say: also because the addressees of this verse are the polytheists of Mecca, and they used to worship idols.

Some of them said: this verse is general for everyone for whom the happiness has preceded from Allah. Muhammad ibn Ḥāṭib said: I heard ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, giving a sermon, and he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom (the best) has preceded﴾, and said: "ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) is among them!"

Al-Junayd said about this verse: "The good fortune (*al-ʿināya*) preceded for them from Allah in the beginning, and the sainthood (*al-wilāya*) appeared in the end."

Abu ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah informed me, saying: Abu al-Ḥusayn Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān al-Nuṣaybī related to us, saying: Abu Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Subaʿī informed us in Aleppo, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār al-Ṣūfī informed us, saying: ʿUbayd Allah al-Qawārīrī related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Abi Yazīd al-Hamadhānī related to us, saying: Layth related to us, from the paternal cousin of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, who was among the entertainers (*summār*) of ʿAlī, who said: One night ʿAlī recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us, those will be kept far away from it﴾. He said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf are among them!" Then the prayer was called, and ʿAlī got up, dragging his cloak, saying: ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾, that is, its sound, when they descend to their dwellings in Paradise. ﴿And they will abide forever in that which their souls desire﴾.

*Al-shahwa* (desire) is the soul's seeking of pleasure. A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Therein is whatever the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾.

﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Abu Ja'far recited *yaḥzunu* with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy. The others recited it with a fatḥa on the yā' and a ḍamma on the zāy. They differed about *al-faza' al-akbar* (the greatest terror). Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the final blast (*al-nafkha al-ākhira*). The evidence is Allah's saying: ﴿And on the Day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills, and all will come to Him in humility﴾.

Al-Ḥasan said: it is when the servant is commanded to go to the Fire.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is when the Fire closes over the people of the Fire.

Ibn Jurayj said: it is when Death is slaughtered in the form of a white-spotted ram on the Heights, while both groups look on. It will be called out: "O people of Paradise, eternity without death! O people of the Fire, eternity without death!"

Dhu al-Nūn al-Miṣrī said: it is separation, abandonment and parting.

﴿And the angels will receive them﴾, meaning they will meet them at the gates of Paradise, congratulating them and saying to them: ﴿This is your day, which you were promised﴾.

﴿On the Day We will roll up the heaven﴾. Abu Ja'far recited *tuṭwā al-samāʾu* (تُطْوَى السَّماءُ) with a ḍamma on the tā' and the hamza, in the passive voice. The others recited it with a nūn, *naṭwī al-samāʾa* (نَطْوِي السَّماءَ), with the accusative on *al-samāʾa*.

﴿Like the rolling up of the scroll for the writings (lil-kutub)﴾. The people of Kufa recited *lil-kutubi* in the plural. Others recited *lil-kitābi* in the singular.

They differed about *al-sijill* (the scroll). Ibn 'Umar and al-Suddī said: *al-sijill* is an angel who writes the deeds of the servants. When it ascends with the seeking of forgiveness, Allah, glorified is He, says: "Write it as light."

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is a sheet (ṣaḥīfa). The *lām* in *lil-kutub* means "upon," according to this interpretation, like folding a sheet over what is written on it.

Abu al-Jawzā' and ʿIkrima related from Ibn ʿAbbās that *al-sijill* is the name of a scribe of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This view is not strong, because the scribes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were well known, and I have mentioned them in my book *al-Rabīʿ*. *Al-sijill* is a noun derived from *al-musājala*, which means mutual writing. Its root is *al-sajl*, which is the bucket. It is said: "I pulled a bucket for the man (*sajjaltu al-rajula*)" when I drew a bucket and he drew a bucket. Then the term was borrowed, and mutual writing and mutual correspondence were called *musājala*. The poet said:

*man yusājilunī yusājil mājidan ... yamlaʾu al-dalwa ilā ʿaqdi al-karab*

"Whoever competes with me in drawing buckets will compete with a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

Then this name was formed on the pattern *faʿl*, like *ṭamr* and *qalz*.

The word *al-ṭayy* (rolling up) in this verse may have two meanings. First, folding, which is the opposite of unfolding, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾.

Second, concealing, obscuring, erasing and effacing, because Allah, glorified is He, will erase its traces and dim its stars, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿When the sun is wrapped up, and when the stars fall﴾. The Arabs say: "Conceal (*uṭwi*) this news about so-and-so," meaning hide it and keep it secret.

Then He began a new statement, saying, Mighty is He Who speaks: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾. Most scholars said: just as We began them in the wombs of their mothers, barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, so We will return them on the Day of Resurrection. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, and His saying: ﴿They will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time"﴾.

The evidence for this interpretation is what Layth related from Mujahid, from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon me while there was an old woman of the Banu ʿĀmir with me. He said: "Who is this old woman, O ʿĀʾisha?" I said: "One of my maternal aunts." She said: "Ask Allah to admit me to Paradise." He said: "Indeed, Paradise is not entered by old women." The old woman was overcome by distress. He said (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah will create them a creation different from their creation. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed We have created them a (special) creation﴾, the verse." Then he said: "They will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection naked, barefoot and uncircumcised. The first to be clothed will be Ibrahim, peace be upon him."

ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her and with her father, said: "Alas for her shame! Will men not be ashamed before one another?" He said: ﴿For every one of them that Day there will be a matter that will occupy him﴾. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾, like the day his mother bore him.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: He says: "We will destroy everything as it was the first time." It was also said: "As We began it from water, We will return it from dust."

﴿A promise upon Us﴾. It is in the accusative as an infinitive (*maṣdar*), meaning: "We promised it, a promise upon Us." ﴿Indeed We are ever doing it﴾, meaning the return and the resurrection.

﴿And We had already written in the Psalms (*al-Zabūr*) after the Reminder (*al-dhikr*)﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza recited *al-Zubūri* with a ḍamma on the zāy. The others recite it with a fatḥa, and it means *al-mazbūr* (the written), like *al-ḥalūb* and *al-rukūb*. It is said: "I wrote the book (*zabartu al-kitāba*) and *dhabartuhu*" when I wrote it.

They differed about the meaning of *al-zabūr* in this verse. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: by *al-zabūr* is meant the revealed books, and by *al-dhikr* (the Reminder) is meant the Mother of the Book, which is with Him.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: *al-dhikr* is the Torah, and *al-zabūr* refers to the revealed books after the Torah.

Al-Shaʿbī said: *al-Zabūr* is the book of Dawud (David), and *al-dhikr* is the Torah.

Some scholars said: "The Zabur is the Zabur of Dawud (David), and the Dhikr is the Qur'an." "Ba'd" here means "qabl" (before), as in His saying: ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾ [Surah al-Kahf 18:79], meaning "in front of them." And His saying: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [Surah al-Nazi'at 79:30], meaning "before that."

﴿That the earth﴾ means the land of Paradise. ﴿My righteous servants shall inherit it﴾ means the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is the view of Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliyah. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the earth"﴾ [Surah al-Zumar 39:74].

Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant that the earth in this world will become the possession of the believers. This is a ruling from Allah, the Exalted, of the manifestation of the religion, the strengthening of the Muslims, and the subjugation of the disbelievers.

Wahb said: "I read in several of the books of Allah that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Indeed I shall cause to inherit the earth My righteous servants from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).'"

﴿Indeed, in this is a message﴾ meaning a means of reaching the desired goal. Whoever follows the Qur'an and acts upon it reaches what he hopes for in reward. Thus the Qur'an is the provision for Paradise, like the provision of a traveller.

﴿For a people who worship﴾ meaning believers who worship Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "[It means] those who have knowledge." Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "They are the community of Muhammad, the people of the five prayers and of the month of Ramadan; Allah, the Exalted, named them 'worshippers'."

﴿And We have not sent you, O Muhammad, except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ Ibn Zayd said: "It means the believers specifically." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is general: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, mercy is written for him in this world and the Hereafter; and whoever does not believe is spared from what befell the nations of transformation, sinking into the earth, and hurling of stones."

﴿Say, "It is only revealed to me that your god is one God; so will you submit?" And if they turn away, say, "I have announced to you on equal terms,"﴾ meaning: I have informed you clearly that between me and you there is war and no peace, and that I oppose your religion. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿on equal terms﴾ is that in the warning I have not favoured some of you with something I concealed from others. And it was said: that you may be equal in belief in it. This is among the eloquent expressions of the Qur'an.

﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ meaning the Resurrection. It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya' 21:97 in some readings; cf. commentary].

﴿Indeed, He knows what is said openly and knows what you conceal. And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾ "Perhaps" here means: perhaps the delay of punishment from you is a trial for you, a test, to see how you act, though He is more knowing. ﴿And provision for a time﴾ means until a term at which Allah decides what He wills.

Abu Bakr al-Juzqi informed us: Abu al-'Abbas al-Da'uli informed us: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Khaythamah informed us: Muhammad ibn Abi Ghalib informed us: Hisham informed us: Mujalid informed us: al-Sab'i informed me: When al-Hasan ibn 'Ali handed over the affair to Mu'awiyah, Mu'awiyah said to him, "Stand up, deliver a sermon, and apologise to the people." Al-Hasan stood and gave a sermon; he praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "Indeed the shrewdest of the shrewd is piety, and the most foolish of foolishness is immorality. And this matter over which I and Mu'awiyah disagreed is either the right of a man who had more right to it, or a right that was mine which I left, seeking the reconciliation of this community." Then he said: ﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾

﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ That is: "Decide between me and those who denied me with truth." Allah does not judge except with truth. There are two interpretations regarding it:

The people of exegesis said: "The truth here means the punishment, as though he sought punishment quickly for his people, and they were punished on the day of Badr and its night." A parallel is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 7:89].

Qatadah said: "When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) witnessed battle, he would say: 'My Lord, judge with truth.'"

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the meaning is "My Lord, judge by Your true judgment," so the word "judgment" is omitted and "truth" is put in its place.

The readers differed concerning this verse. Hafs read ﴿Qala﴾ with an alif, as a statement. The rest read "Qul" as a command. Abu Ja'far read "Rabbu" with a damma on the ba' as a vocative and a definite noun. al-Dahhak and Ya'qub read "Rabbi uhkum" with the yā' affirmed, in the sense of a statement that Allah is the most just of all judges; this reading is not accepted because it contradicts the codex (mushaf). The remaining readers read ﴿Rabbi uhkum﴾ as a supplication.

﴿And our Lord, the Most Merciful, is the One sought for help against what you describe.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 21, verses 95–112 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And forbidden is (for) a town﴾. The people of Kufa recited *wa-ḥimrun* (وَحِرْمٌ) with a kasra on the ḥa' and a sukun on the ra', without an alif. The others recited *wa-ḥarāmun* (وَحَرامٌ). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Ḥatim preferred this second reading. Both are dialectal variants, like *ḥill* and *ḥalāl*.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of the verse, ﴿And forbidden is (for) a town whom We have destroyed﴾, is that its people will not return after destruction. According to this interpretation, the *lā* (لا) is extra (*ṣila*), as in the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

*fī sirrin lā ḥūrā sarā wa-mā shaʿar*

meaning: "in a well, not ... he travelled by night and did not perceive," that is, "in a well of ḥūr."

Others said: *al-ḥarām* here means *al-wājib* (obligatory), as in the verse of al-Khansa':

*wa-inna ḥarāman lā arā al-dahra bākiyan ʿalā shajwihi illā bakaytu ʿalā ʿAmr*

"Indeed, it is obligatory that I never see anyone weeping over his grief through time except that I weep over ʿAmr." According to this interpretation, *lā* is an affirmative particle (*thābit*).

Jabir al-Ju'fi said: I asked Abu Ja'far about the return (*al-raj'a*), and he recited this verse.

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾. The majority recited *futiḥat* (فُتِحَتْ) with light emphasis. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub recited it with emphasis, *futtiḥat* (فُتِّحَتْ), on the kasra. The meaning of the verse is that the barrier is opened for Gog and Magog (*Yājūj wa-Mājūj*). We have already explained their story in the commentary.

Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir related from Rib'i ibn Khirash, from Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first of the signs are the Dajjal (the Antichrist), the descent of ʿIsa (Jesus), a fire that comes out of the bottom of Aden in Yemen and drives people toward the place of assembly, staying with them at night when they rest, the smoke, the beast (*al-dābba*), and then Gog and Magog."

Ḥudhayfa said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, what are Gog and Magog?" He said: "They are nations. Each nation is four hundred thousand nations. A man among them does not die until he sees a thousand eyes blinking before him from his own loins. They are the children of Adam (peace be upon him). They march toward the ruin of the world. Their vanguard will be in Syria and their rear in Iraq. They pass by the rivers of the world and drink the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Sea of Tiberias, until they come to Jerusalem. They say, 'We have killed the people of the world,' so they fight whoever is in the heaven. They shoot arrows toward the sky, and their arrows return to them stained with blood, and they say, 'We have killed those in the heaven.'"

ʿIsa and the Muslims are at the Mount of Sinai (*Ṭūr Sīnīn*). Allah, glorified is He, reveals to ʿIsa: "Take My servants into the mountain and what is near it." Then ʿIsa raises his hands to the sky, and the Muslims say, "Amen." Allah sends upon them a worm called *al-Naghf* (in the copy of Isfahan: *al-ʿArf*), which enters their nostrils. They become dead from the farthest part of Syria to the farthest part of the East (in Tafsir al-Tabari: Iraq; in the copy of Isfahan: the West), until the earth stinks from their corpses. Allah commands the sky, and it rains like the mouths of waterskins, washing the earth of their corpses and stench. At that time, the sun rises from the west."

﴿And they, from every hill (ḥadab), are swarming﴾. *Ḥadab* means a rise and a hill. *Yanselūn* means they come out walking swiftly, like the rapid gait of a wolf.

The scholars differed about this pronoun. One group said it refers to Gog and Magog, and they cited the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Gog and Magog will be let loose, and they will come out upon the people, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿from every hill they swarm﴾, and they will overrun the earth."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), regarding what is mentioned about ʿIsa, who said: "ʿIsa said: My Lord has commanded me that the Dajjal will come out, and that I will descend to him. It is mentioned that he has two canes. When he sees me, Allah will destroy him." He said: "He will melt as lead melts, until even the tree and the stone will say, 'O Muslim, this is a disbeliever, so kill him.' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will destroy them, and people will return to their lands and homelands. Then Gog and Magog will come to them ﴿from every hill swarming﴾. They will not pass over anything without destroying it, and they will not pass over water without drinking it."

Others said: the pronoun refers to all creation, meaning that they will come out of their graves and places and be gathered to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. This is supported by Mujahid's recitation, *wa-hum min kulli jadathin* (وَهُمْ مِنْ كُلِّ جَدَثٍ), with a jim and a tha', meaning the grave, based on Allah's saying: ﴿So, when they come out from the graves to their Lord, they swarm﴾.

﴿And the true promise draws near﴾, meaning the Resurrection. Al-Farra' (a grammarian) and a group of scholars said: the *wāw* in ﴿and draws near﴾ is superfluous (*muqḥam*), and the meaning of the verse is: "Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, the true promise draws near." A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿So when they both had submitted, and he had laid him down upon his forehead, and We called out to him﴾, meaning "We called out to him." Imru' al-Qays said:

*fa-lammā ajznā sāḥata al-ḥayyi wa-ntaḥā bi-bāṭini khabtin dhī qifāfin ʿaqanqali*

"When we passed the open area of the tribe and he turned aside into the bottom of a valley with ridges and winding sand hills," meaning *intaḥā* (he turned aside). The evidence for this interpretation is the hadith of Ḥudhayfa, who said: "If a man kept a colt after the emergence of Gog and Magog, he would not ride it until the Hour is established."

Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian) said: The Basrans do not permit omitting the *wāw*, and they make the answer of *ḥattā idhā futiḥat* (until, when ... are opened) to be ﴿They say: O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾. The verse would then be: ﴿until, when Gog and Magog are let loose ... and the true promise draws near, they say: O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾.

﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾. In the phrase ﴿it﴾ (*hiya*) there are three possibilities:

First, *hiya* may refer to *al-abṣār* (the eyes), and *al-abṣār* (the eyes) that follows may be an explanation of it, as in the verse of a poet:

*la-ʿamru abīhā lā taqūlu ẓaʿīnatī ... alā firra ʿannī mālikun ibnu Abī Kaʿbi*

"By the life of her father, my she-camel does not say, 'Ah, flee from me, Malik ibn Abi Kaʿb.'" Here the poet refers to the camel (*ẓaʿīna*) by the pronoun in *abīhā* and then makes it explicit. So the meaning of the statement is: "Then, the eyes are staring fixedly, the eyes of those who disbelieved."

Second, *hiya* may be a dummy pronoun (*ʿimād*), as in Allah's saying: ﴿For indeed it is not the eyes that go blind﴾, and as in the verse of a poet: "So is it raised by what is here, a head?"

Third, the sentence may end at *hiya*, meaning "it is present, standing," that is, it is so near that it is as if it is coming and present. Then a new sentence begins: *shākhiṣatun abṣāru alladhīna kafarū* (the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring fixedly), with the predicate placed before the subject. The meaning is: the eyes of those who disbelieved are staring fixedly from the terror of the Hour's standing. They say: ﴿O woe to us! We were heedless of this﴾, that is, of this day. ﴿Nay, we were wrongdoers﴾, by disobeying our Lord and placing worship in other than its proper place.

﴿Indeed you, O polytheists, and what you worship besides Allah﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿are fuel (ḥaṣab) for Hell﴾. The common recitation is with a ṣād (حَصَبُ). It means its fuel, according to Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima said: it means its firewood. It is mentioned that *ḥaṣab* in the dialect of the people of Yemen means firewood.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means they will be thrown into the Fire as pebbles are thrown. The root *ḥaṣb* means throwing. It is said: "I pelted the man (*ḥaṣabtu al-rajula*) when I threw at him." Allah, Glorified, said: ﴿Indeed We sent against them a violent wind (ḥāṣiban)﴾, meaning a wind that pelts them with stones. Ibn 'Abbas recited *ḥaḍab* with a ḍād (حَضَبُ), which is everything with which the fire is kindled and fanned. From this the fine sparks of fire are called *ḥaḍab*.

ʿAli and ʿAʾisha recited (the word) with a ṭāʾ, *ḥaṭab* (حَطَبُ), meaning firewood.

A parallel is Allah's saying: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾.

﴿You will be its (*lahā*) inhabitants (wāridūn)﴾, meaning you will enter it. ﴿If these idols were gods in reality, they would not have entered it﴾, meaning their worshippers would not have entered the Fire; rather, the idols would have protected them. ﴿And each one in it will abide forever﴾, meaning the worshipper and the worshipped.

﴿For them therein is wailing, and they will not hear therein﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said about this verse: When those who will remain forever in the Fire are left in it, they will be placed in coffins of fire. Then these coffins are placed inside other coffins, and those inside still others, and the coffins have nails of fire. They will not hear anything, and no one among them will see that there is anyone else in the Fire being punished.

Then He made an exception, saying, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (reward) has preceded from Us﴾. Some scholars said: *inna* here means *illā* (except), and there is no other instance of this in the Qur'an. *Al-sabq* means one thing preceding another.

﴿For them, from Us, is the best (*al-ḥusnā*)﴾, meaning happiness, the good promise, and the beautiful reward of Paradise. ﴿They will be kept far away from it (mubʿadūn)﴾. *Al-ibʿād* means increasing the distance.

They differed about who these people are. Most exegetes said: they are those who worship something besides Allah while they are obedient to it, and the worship of those who worship it is hateful to them. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the chiefs of Quraysh were in the Ḥaṭīm, around the Kaʿba, and there were three hundred and sixty idols. He sat with them. Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith approached him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) silenced him by argument. Then he recited to him and to them: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, the three verses. Then he stood up. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zabaʿrā ibn Qays ibn ʿAdī al-Sahmī came and saw them whispering. He said: "What is your discussion?" Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to them. ʿAbd Allah said: "By Allah, if I had found him, I would have refuted him." They called the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Ibn al-Zabaʿrā said to him: "Did you say: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I have refuted you, by the Lord of the Kaʿba! Do not the Jews worship ʿUzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes, rather they worship the devils, who commanded them to do so." Then Allah, Glorified, revealed: ﴿Indeed those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾, the verse, meaning ʿUzayr, ʿIsa and the angels.

Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl said: By His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, He meant only the idols and not others, because if He had meant the angels and people, He would have said *man taʿbudūna* (who you worship). I say: also because the addressees of this verse are the polytheists of Mecca, and they used to worship idols.

Some of them said: this verse is general for everyone for whom the happiness has preceded from Allah. Muhammad ibn Ḥāṭib said: I heard ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, giving a sermon, and he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed those for whom (the best) has preceded﴾, and said: "ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) is among them!"

Al-Junayd said about this verse: "The good fortune (*al-ʿināya*) preceded for them from Allah in the beginning, and the sainthood (*al-wilāya*) appeared in the end."
